articles.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
articles.summary:
Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze

Senior Sudanese…

blocks.text: Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

articles.title: Catholic bishops accuse Trump White House of turning prayer into campaign photo op
articles.summary:
Two bishops express regret after the White House posts photos and video of a prayer with them in the Oval Office

Two Catholic bishops who bowed their heads with Donald Trump in the Oval…

blocks.text: Two Catholic bishops who bowed their heads with Donald Trump in the Oval Office now say they regret it, accusing the White House of turning a private prayer into a campaign photo opportunity before next week’s US elections.

Archbishop Jeffrey Grob of Milwaukee and bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, who were among the 12 bishops who met administration officials last Thursday, issued separate statements of regret over the weekend.

The fallout stems from the White House quickly posting video and photos of the prayer on social media, captioned as Catholic archbishops and bishops praying with the US president, less than two weeks before the midterm elections on 3 November.

Archbishop Grob issued a statement headlined A Public Apology, in which he said he felt “a heavy sadness” over the pain the images had caused, and that he had heard from people alarmed that he had unwittingly joined a political event on the eve of a national vote.

Others, he said, were hurt because of the effect of Trump’s policies on their families. “We should never have been put in that position by the White House,” wrote Grob, adding that he had harbored reservations and “wish I had heeded them”.
Bishop Joensen wrote that “many things tied to this present Administration” were “blatantly at odds with our Catholic faith”.

He said none of the bishops was unaware the meeting fell close to an election, but insisted that none had intended to endorse a party or candidate. “I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes.”

Grob said the Heritage Foundation, the conservative thinktank behind the Project 2025 rightwing blueprint for the second Trump administration, arranged the meeting. The bishops, he said, were told it would be a private discussion of immigration enforcement, religious-worker visas and human dignity, with a possible chance to pray privately with the president.

After 90 minutes with domestic policy staff, they were ushered into the Oval Office, handed commemorative tokens and, Grob detailed, directed to stand behind Trump’s desk and pray. Nobody told them a video was being recorded, he said, and they never agreed to its release.

Joensen said officials connected to the White House Faith Office invited him, and that the agenda also covered fertility treatment incentives, abortion-inducing drugs and tax credits for private schools.

Archbishop James Golka of Denver, another participant, told his archdiocese’s publication that he understood why many saw the video as an endorsement but that it was “never my intention”. “I’m heartbroken that people are hurt, and that there are people intentionally using this moment to sow disunity,” he said.

Bishop Scott Bullock of Rapid City told the National Catholic Reporter that a Heritage Foundation representative had invited him and that the US Conference of Catholic Bishops was “not unaware” of the meeting. He did not say who in the leadership knew.

Trump has spent his second term fusing Christian prayers with the machinery of government, creating a White House Faith Office by executive order in February 2025 and, the same month, a justice department-led taskforce to “eradicate anti-Christian bias” in federal agencies.

The president faced criticism in April for posting an AI-generated image on his Truth Social platform depicting himself as a Jesus-like figure. He later deleted the post, and claimed it was “supposed to be me as a doctor making people better”.

At the Pentagon, Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, has held Christian worship services (which the Associated Press reports have been led only by evangelicals) and in March prayed for “overwhelming violence” against “those who deserve no mercy” in the Iran war.

And when the Episcopal bishop Mariann Budde urged him at his inauguration prayer service to show mercy toward migrants and LGBTQ+ people, Trump demanded that she and her church apologize, which she in turn rejected.

Archbishop Paul Coakley of Oklahoma City, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, has urged Catholics to put faith ahead of politics before the vote. The bishops are due to hold their annual fall assembly in Baltimore in November, about two weeks after the election.
“We are, as ever, a pilgrim people,” Grob wrote. “And that includes bishops,”. He ended his apology with “sincere regret”.

articles.title: Russell Brand had ‘insane sexual appetite’ and bad behaviour on ‘another level’, trial told
articles.summary:
Brand, charged with rape and sexual assault, was ‘sleeping with people day and night’, former assistant alleges

Russell Brand had an “insane sexual appetite” and his bad behaviour was on…

blocks.text: Russell Brand had an “insane sexual appetite” and his bad behaviour was on “another level” to that of other celebrities, his former personal assistant has told a court.
Helen Berger told police she had seen Brand treat women badly and that she once had to stop his mother and girlfriend walking in on him having sex with someone in his dressing room.
She also alleged she witnessed the 51-year-old comedian receiving oral sex in a toilet cubicle and once found a celebrity leaving his bedroom in the morning.
Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.
Wearing a grey suit and white shirt, Brand sat still in the dock as statements from prosecution witnesses were read to Southwark crown court on Monday.

Berger worked for Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, when the TV personality was at the height of his fame. She said the job was one of the hardest she had had because Brand had “non-stop energy” and she left because she was “sick of him” and burnt out.

“Though I’d worked with celebrities before and seen a lot of people normalising bad behaviour, this was on another level. I think everyone else normalising and dismissing Russell’s behaviour made me think, I guess, this is just the way it is,” Berger said in the May 2024 police statement.

Describing his behaviour, she added: “He was always in his underwear, he loved walking around in his underwear with no shirt on. I remember Sadie Frost came over to interview him. He did the whole interview in his underwear and no shirt and an open robe.”
At the time Brand had filming commitments for Channel 4’s Big Brother as well as MTV and the BBC, a radio show, a national comedy tour, a weekly Guardian column, and was writing a book.

“In addition to his busy work, he had an insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night. He was very open about what his needs were,” Berger said in the statement that was read by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC.

“He never seemed happy after sex, more so depressed,” Berger alleged. “There were times when I was at his house and he would be on a deadline … and he would get antsy and joke with me: ‘May I go and have sex now?’”

She recalled Brand turning to the website MySpace to find random women to sleep with and how women, including an unnamed celebrity, would often be at his flat in Camden, north London, for sexual liaisons. “He was like a peacock, women always approached him,” she said.
When Brand was recording an MTV show, Berger alleged, he told her to ask women for their telephone numbers, which made her feel uncomfortable.

She alleged that on other occasions she had been made to keep Brand’s mother and girlfriend away from his dressing room because he was having sex, and how she had overheard him receiving oral sex in a women’s toilet. Berger described overhearing Brand talking and recognising his trademark cowboy boots in the cubicle next door.

Berger recalled that when Brand was headlining the Edinburgh festival, he ended his show by asking that anyone with “a vagina and heartbeat” meet him at a pub afterwards. Many women showed up, Berger said, and she later found him having sex in the shower at the apartment he was renting.
“I never witnessed Russell doing anything against the law,” she said, before adding: “I did see Russell treat women poorly.”

She recalled how he was once “hitting on” a woman who revealed she had a boyfriend before Brand “turned in a way” that startled his then PA. “He literally just switched off his charm and moved on to the next woman,” Berger said.

The court also heard a witness statement from the manager of a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Brand when she worked at Channel 4 in 2009. The manager said she recalled the alleged victim telling her that Brand’s associates Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy had “told her she had to give Mr Brand a massage” or he would not continue with the day’s recording.
The manager recalled being told that Bayles and Roy “were both there the whole time and watched and laughed while Mr Brand sexually assaulted her right in front of them”.
The sister of a woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted and then orally raped by Brand at a Soho bar in 2004 told the court she was “upset and almost in shock” the next morning.

In 2023, the woman called her sister in tears and told the “full story” of what had happened, the court heard. “It sounded like she was struggling to catch her breath,” the witness recalled. “She said his [Brand’s] eyes had gone completely black and he was possessed or had been a completely different person.”
The trial continues.

articles.title: Why Ukraine may be involved in Mali's conflict
articles.summary: Allegations that Ukrainian specialists are supporting Tuareg rebels in Mali highlight Kyiv's effort to challenge Russian influence far beyond the battlefield in Europe.

image.caption: There are growing indications that Ukraine is providing military support to Tuareg rebels and jihadists in MaliImage: Souleymane Ag Anara/AFP

blocks.text: Ukraine is fighting Russia — and the conflict may extend into Africa's Sahel region.

According to an investigation published by US media outlet CNN this month, around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists are reportedly supporting Tuareg rebels in northern Mali. Their common enemy: the military government in Bamako and its Russian allies.
But how reliable is the information? And what price could Kyiv pay for engaging in Africa?

Marta Oliynyk-D'omochko, coordinator of the African Studies Program at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, sees a strategic motive. "Ukraine's main interest is to weaken Russia's influence around the world," she told DW. If Russia's military influence were rolled back, she added, the economic opportunities arising from it would also diminish.

Russian historian Irina Filatova, professor emeritus at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, also considers Ukrainian support for the Tuareg movement plausible. However, she says she has no independent evidence to confirm such involvement.

Kyiv's alleged partners are controversial. The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) cooperates with the Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimeen (JNIM), a jihadist group affiliated with al-Qaeda.
Suspicions dating back to 2024
In July 2024, DW reported on possible involvement by the Ukrainian military intelligence service (HUR) in an ambush on Russian Wagner fighters near Tinzaouaten in northern Mali.
At the time, HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov said the Tuareg rebels had received information they needed to carry out the attack. Ukraine denied direct involvement.
Jihadist groups in Africa and their links
Paramilitaries from Russia's Wagner Group and Malian troops suffered heavy losses in the July 2024 attack.
CNN's investigation has reignited the question of whether the Russia-Ukraine war is also being fought on African soil.
Signals from Kyiv, but no confirmation

The suspicions were renewed by a post on X by Kyrylo Budanov. The former head of Ukraine's military intelligence, now chief of staff to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on September 7 that Ukrainian intelligence protects the country's interests worldwide — "from Russia to Africa … in the burning desert sands and in the snows of icy Antarctica...".

Budanov did not explicitly mention Mali and his post does not confirm any specific operation. CNN reported that the Ukrainians provided drone training, operational planning and remote support for drone missions. DW has not independently verified those claims.

DW reached out to the HUR for comment. Among other things, DW wanted to know whether personnel had been deployed to Mali, whether the political leadership had approved such a mission, and what measures were in place to ensure that the JNIM — which cooperates with the FLA — does not indirectly benefit from Ukrainian support.
DW did not receive a specific response. An HUR spokesperson said the agency might provide information at a later date. The extent of any potential Ukrainian involvement therefore remains unclear.
Why Mali matters to Kyiv

Following military coups in 2020 and 2021, Mali increasingly turned away from Western partners and toward Russia. The Wagner Group was subsequently replaced by the Africa Corps in 2025 as Moscow reorganized its military presence.
Russia has sought to consolidate its influence in the Sahel region and present itself as a reliable security partner.
Ulf Laessing, former head of the Sahel program of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Mali and now head of Konrad's Syria and Iraq program, says Russia is continuing to expand its activities in Africa.

"I have received information that the Africa Corps still uses Syria and Libya as transit points for flights from Russia, including for refueling and loading, to support its operations on the continent," Laessing told DW.
How could Wagner Group revolt impact Africa?
From Ukraine's perspective, it could be attractive to exert pressure on Russian forces in Africa.

Filatova sees a strategic logic to this: "The Ukrainians regard Russian troops anywhere in the world as legitimate targets." Setbacks in Mali could tie up Russian resources and undermine Moscow's reputation as a security partner, she argued.

However, Oliynyk-D'omochko stresses that the relationship with the Tuareg is not a comprehensive alliance. The FLA is not seeking to replace the government in Bamako. Instead, it is focused on northern Mali and is pursuing self-determination or extensive autonomy.
Oliynyk-D'omochko describes the relationship as a tactical arrangement: "It is more of a situational alliance against a common enemy than a comprehensive partnership."
The alliance with jihadists

The FLA is fighting for an independent state in the north of Mali, a region predominantly inhabited by Tuaregs. JNIM, by contrast, aims to impose strict Islamic rule. Both groups oppose the military government and its Russian allies, but their objectives differ.

Any potential Ukrainian support for the FLA would not, in itself, prove that Kyiv is directly supporting JNIM. However, jihadists could benefit indirectly if they conduct joint operations with FLA or gain access to knowledge and equipment.
Cooperation between Tuareg and Islamist groups dates back more than a decade.

After the ousting and killing of Libya's longtime dictator Muammar al-Gaddafi during the Arab Spring in October 2011, heavily armed Tuareg fighters returned to Mali and took up the struggle for an independent state.
In the process, separatist ambitions became intertwined with Islamist movements. Iyad Ag Ghaly, the current leader of JNIM, was himself involved in the Tuareg rebellion before turning to jihadism.

According to Oliynyk-D'omochko, the cooperation is primarily tactical in nature. The two sides have collaborated during past uprisings but later fell out. It remains unclear how long the current alliance will last.

For Kyiv, this also poses a political risk. In many African countries, the Tuaregs are viewed as separatists. Cooperation with them could therefore create the impression that Ukraine is interfering in another country's internal affairs.
Claims of support for armed groups

Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso accuse Ukraine of supporting armed groups and threatening their territorial integrity. The three Sahel nations, all ruled by military governments, have severed diplomatic relations with Kyiv and deepened their cooperation with Russia.

In September, Mali's Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop accused Ukraine at the United Nations of "providing clear and open support to terrorist groups and other mafia-like groups to undermine our country's territorial integrity," reported Agence France-Presse. Diop did not provide evidence for his claim.
The three nations' governments have may have an interest in legitimizing their partnership with Moscow and portraying Kyiv as a destabilizing actor.
Filatova considers Ukrainian activities in the region plausible but says she has no evidence to substantiate the accusations.

Oliynyk-D'omochko has likewise found no definitive proof. At the same time, she warns of the potential consequences for Ukraine's Africa policy: Kyiv advocates equal partnerships with African countries. Any alleged cooperation with separatists could undermine that message and affect how potential partners view Ukraine.
What price could Ukraine pay?

Engagement in Mali could offer Ukraine a relatively low-cost way to weaken Russian interests beyond Europe. A small team of specialists could train local fighters and improve their capabilities in the use of drones.

But a potential partnership with the FLA carries political risks. Because the Tuareg separatists cooperate with the JNIM, Kyiv could face accusations of indirectly supporting Islamist fighters. That could undermine Ukraine's efforts to strengthen its relations with African countries.

articles.title: Part of Antarctica named after former BBC science correspondent
articles.summary: A stretch of water in the west of the continent is now called the Amos Channel after the ex-BBC journalist.

blocks.text: The melting ice sheets of this remote continent are just one of many aspects of polar science that Amos reported on while at the BBC. He also covered colossal icebergs, the fate of penguin colonies and a BBC exclusive about the discovery of Ernest Shackleton's lost ship, the Endurance.
"It's absolutely incredible - what an extraordinary accolade. I'm so touched that there's a little bit of Antarctica named after me," Amos said.
Despite his fascination with the South Pole, he has not yet travelled to the continent.
"I've written about it so often, but always from my desk - this is quite the incentive to go and visit.
"Antarctica is the front line of the biggest news story on planet Earth - climate change," he added.
The naming of geographical features in Antarctica follows strict rules.

The Amos Channel was recommended by the UK Antarctic Place Names Committee, which looks after names for sites within the British Antarctic Territory, as well as South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.
Athena Dinar, from the British Antarctic Survey, said: "Jon's passion for Antarctica and engaging journalism offers something for every reader, viewer or listener.
"The naming of an Antarctic place in his honour is a fitting recognition of his outstanding contribution to the promotion of Antarctic research."

Amos joined the BBC in 1986 as a local radio reporter in Cambridge. He was part of the team that launched the BBC News website in 1997, and ran the online science desk for many years. He later worked as a BBC science correspondent across TV, radio and online, before leaving the organisation in 2024.

"Jon consistently highlighted the importance of Antarctic research, explaining not only what science is being done there, but why it matters for society, climate understanding and the global environment," said Fiona Fox, from the Science Media Centre.

articles.title: Audi boss under fire in Germany for Trump rally appearance
articles.summary:
Gernot Döllner criticised for in-person announcement of major investment in US days before midterm elections

The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a…

blocks.text: The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a rally with Donald Trump just days before the US midterm elections, to announce billions of dollars of investment in battleground state Georgia.

Gernot Döllner joined Trump on stage after the US president gave a speech criticised by the head of an elected body of employees at Audi’s parent company, Volkswagen, as being full of “racism, sexism, transphobia [and] contempt for democracy”.

Daniela Cavallo, the head of the VW works council, added that anyone who heard Trump’s speech and then saw that Döllner had become an active participant in the event must “sink into the ground with shame”, according to internal company communications released to German media.
She said the investment deal and Döllner’s appearance showed VW’s management had allowed itself to be “turned into a puppet in the propaganda show of a highly dubious political figure”.

Isabel Cademartori, the transport spokesperson for Germany’s Social Democrats – part of the country’s ruling coalition – called Döllner’s actions a “disgrace”. She added this was particularly so “in view of the history of the Volkswagen Group”, in an apparent reference to VW’s founding as a showcase company under the Nazis.

A spokesperson for the German government declined to comment on the matter, calling it “a business decision regarding where the company invests and, in this case, where the company’s chief executive appears”.

blocks.caption: Döllner announced plans to spend $4bn and create 4,500 jobs in the battleground state of Georgia. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP

blocks.text: Döllner and Trump announced to the crowd on Saturday that Audi would spend $4bn to build its first factory in the US and create 4,500 jobs, even as VW aims to slash tens of thousands of positions and close plants in Germany.

“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Döllner said at the rally in Perry near Macon, in a highly unusual move for a European executive during a hard-fought US electoral campaign.
He called the plans, which foresee factory construction starting next year and car production beginning in the 2030s, “a long-term investment because we believe in the American market”.

Audi is the only premium car manufacturer without its own factory in the US, making it particularly vulnerable to Trump’s punishing 15% import tariffs, which cost it an estimated €1.2bn last year. The Macon plant would build 200,000 SUVs annually.

The head of the powerful German trade union IG Metall, Christiane Benner, called Döllner’s US appearance “extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company, but above all of Audi’s employees”.
She accused Döllner of being in “flagrant breach” of the company’s code of conduct, “which expressly requires political neutrality in the run-up to elections”.
She warned that any major investment like the Macon plant would have to go before VW’s supervisory board. Benner is the board’s deputy chair.
after newsletter promotion

Volkswagen is currently locked in a battle between management and labour over a push to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the downsizing on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as US tariffs and the expensive transition to electric vehicles.

Its German ​factories are under particular pressure to drive down costs, with Audi’s facility in Neckarsulm, which employs 15,000 people, among four VW plants threatened with closure from early next decade.
“Each site must do its part in terms of competitiveness and the long-term strength of Audi,” a company spokesperson said.

Trump is deeply unpopular in Germany and has riled its political mainstream by vocally backing the far-right Alternative für Deutschland. The AfD is the country’s most popular party according to polls, and has actively courted Trump’s support.

The 3 November election in Georgia could be decisive in the Democrats’ battle to regain a majority in the Senate. The incumbent senator, Jon Ossoff, is fighting a tough re-election battle against Republican challenger Mike Collins, in a state Trump won in 2024.
Trump has argued ahead of the midterms that his tariffs on car imports are helping the US economy.

articles.title: Unions suspend planned V&A strike after improved pay offer
articles.summary:
London sites to remain open as Prospect and PCS agree to ‘Acas-facilitated talks’ with museum management

A planned strike at the V&A over half-term has been suspended after an improved…

blocks.text: A planned strike at the V&A over half-term has been suspended after an improved offer from its management.

Museum staff who were members of the Prospect and Public and Commercial Services (PCS) unions had voted to strike on Thursday and Friday in a dispute over pay and working conditions including inadequate toilet and hydration breaks. The strike would have closed the V&A’s main galleries in south Kensington, as well as V&A East, V&A Storehouse and Young V&A in east London.
The strike was suspended on Monday pending last-minute talks with the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service, after the V&A management made an improved offer.

In a statement PCS said it had suspended strikes planned for 29 and 30 October “to allow Acas-facilitated talks to take place, following an improved offer from the museum”. Prospect and the V&A also confirmed the strike had been suspended while negotiations continued.

The unions are demanding a 4% pay increase for staff earning above the living wage, and for the V&A to become an accredited London living-wage employer within 12 months. They also want time-and-a-half pay for bank holiday working.

On conditions, they are seeking improvements to working during heatwaves and better food at the museum’s east London sites. In July, when staff first voted to strike, a V&A spokesperson said “extensive measures” had been introduced to help staff during the heatwave. These included additional rest breaks and closing some galleries during the hottest periods.
The dispute has previously involved two separate two-day strikes in September.

blocks.caption: V&A East Storehouse, east London. ‘All V&A museums will be open this week,’ a spokesperson said.  Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: A V&A spokesperson said: “All V&A museums will be open this week, including all exhibitions, free displays and planned half-term activities. While we are working to reinstate as much of our public programme as possible, unfortunately some events may still be cancelled or postponed – visitors are encouraged to check our website before travelling.

“We welcome this opportunity for constructive discussions with our trade union colleagues. Our latest pay offer delivers an average 4.18% pay rise and a 6.9% increase for our lowest-paid colleagues; increased bank holiday pay to 1.5, alongside a sector-leading bonus scheme and a subsidised food offer for staff at all V&A sites.”
Paula Lamont, Prospect’s national secretary, said: “We will be entering talks in good faith and hope that a resolution to the dispute can be found.”
Earlier this month, Prospect’s general secretary, Mike Clancy, called on the V&A’s director, Tristram Hunt, a former Labour MP, to get involved in the negotiations.

He said: “Prospect members are dedicated to their jobs, and it is these dedicated staff who make the museum the world-class attraction it is. That Tristram Hunt can’t even be bothered to take part in the negotiations himself shows the level of disdain in which he holds his staff.”

The London living wage is now £15.45 an hour. While the V&A has said all its staff are paid at least this rate, some of the museum’s outsourced contractors are not. V&A Dundee, which is not involved in the dispute, is an accredited living-wage employer.

articles.title: Gamers, developers praise BioWare's envelope-pushing games following 'heartbreaking' closure
articles.summary: Gamers, developers and critics lamented the closure of revered studio BioWare, with many crediting its works for kickstarting their own careers in the games industry.

image.caption: A promotional image for Mass Effect 3, developed by Edmonton-based video game studio BioWare. (BioWare/Electronic Arts)

blocks.text: To video game players, developers and industry watchers, the sudden closure of Edmonton-based BioWare came as a shock but not necessarily a surprise.

"I knew BioWare wasn't long for this world, so I had already done my mourning for that studio. And so when this news came down, I was like, yep, that's pretty much what I expected," said Ash Parrish, a writer for the gaming news site Kotaku. "This sucks super hard."
The studio, founded in Edmonton in 1995 by three doctors and acquired by U.S.-based games publisher Electronic Arts in 2007, was shuttered as part of company-wide layoffs on Wednesday.
Its developers specialized in role-playing games with a heavy emphasis on storytelling and player agency, including Baldur's Gate, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age and Mass Effect.

"Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this news, along with their families and colleagues. Canada’s video game industry is home to an exceptional depth of talent and creativity, and the contributions of the people who built BioWare will remain an important part of our industry’s story," said Paul Fogolin, president of the Entertainment Software Association of Canada, in a statement.

Gamers, developers and critics lamented the news online, with many crediting its works for kickstarting their own careers in the games industry. They also noted that while BioWare may be no more, its impact on video games will continue into the future.
Financial pressures after Saudi buyout

The recent fortunes of EA made BioWare's closure less shocking. BioWare's staff was slashed from about 200 to less than half that in 2025, after Dragon Age: The Veilguard failed to meet internal sales expectations.

Earlier this year, Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund and a private equity firm owned by U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner finalized a $55-billion US buyout of EA. It included $20 billion borrowed from U.S. bank JPMorgan, which now hangs over EA as leveraged debt.

Alyssa Mercante, a digital trends writer for Digiday and a former games journalist, said EA likely thought it was more important to maintain its "biggest moneymakers," like sports games and online multiplayer shooters with live service elements, than the titles with a "lengthy development cycle" and the deep role-playing games (RPGs) that BioWare is known for.
The Edmonton-based video game company BioWare is being shut down

Live service games offer additional content, which can sometimes include randomized trading card-like content packs, that costs more money or subscriptions on top of the initial retail price. EA credited live service games like Battlefield 6 and the soccer franchise EA Sports FC for reaching live service revenues of $1.47 billion US in the previous quarter.
RPGs like Dragon Age or Mass Effect, meanwhile, are sold like a single book or movie, with few avenues for additional monetized content.
Groundbreaking narrative, diverse stories and characters

BioWare's games have long been celebrated for featuring characters of diverse gender identities and backgrounds. For example, players can choose whether the main character Shepard in Mass Effect or Hawke in Dragon Age is male or female. Some games also have optional same-sex romantic storylines between main characters and narratives featuring transgender characters.
Gaming writer Parrish credits Dragon Age: Origins (2009) for pulling her out of an emotionally difficult time in her life.
"I'm like, let me try it and see, you know, if this sparks joy. And it did," she said. "It just rewrote my brain chemistry in ways that I'm still experiencing ... to this day."
A promotional screenshot from Dragon Age: The Veilguard. (BioWare/Electronic Arts)
She credits it for inspiring her to become a games journalist and Dragon Age fan communities online for connecting her with lifelong friends who would go on to attend her wedding years later.
Mercante had a similar journey when she first played Dragon Age's sci-fi sister series Mass Effect.
"It had wrapped itself around my core personality and kind of stayed there for a while in my teens, early 20s," she said.
Voice actor Jennifer Hale is photographed in her studio on Vancouver Island, B.C., in 2024. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)
Players at the outset chose whether to play as a male Shephard, voiced by Mark Meer, or "FemShep" (as she's known by fans), played by Vancouver Island-based Jennifer Hale.

"Being FemShep means an enormous amount to me," said Hale, who called it "an extraordinary privilege" to play a main character whose female version was treated on an equal footing as her male counterpart.
"That means the world to me. I love me some kicking down barriers."

items: ‘Part of the city’s DNA’: Former BioWare writer reflects on company's impact on Edmonton

blocks.text: Natalie Checo, a Vancouver-based video game designer originally from the U.S., says she connected particularly with the genetically enhanced operative Miranda Lawson in Mass Effect 2.

"What resonated for me was the story about a woman who is biologically engineered to be perfect, and yet she still can't really attain that, because being perfect is a human impossibility," she said. "I think women grow up in a society that pushes us to be as perfect as possible."
Checo says that many of her game developer friends are from marginalized communities, and BioWare's games "pushed us to dream more than our real world has allowed us to feel like we can."
Ongoing legacy
Osama Dorias, a Montreal-based developer at HeartLoop Games, says BioWare's games taught him important lessons when working on narrative-based games of his own.
"I played Mass Effect 1, and I was really surprised by the level of agency that they were able to give the protagonist Shepard, and how the characters still had their own personality," he said.
Varric the dwarf and Solas the elf are seen in Dragon Age: Inquisition. (BioWare/Electronic Arts)

Dorias, Mercante and others pointed to successful RPGs by other studios that have carried on that format, including CD Projekt Red's The Witcher series and Baldur's Gate 3, a direct sequel to BioWare's games of the same name made by Belgian studio Larian.
Dorias calls BioWare's closing "heartbreaking," estimating that at its peak, the company may have employed half of all full-time employees in Edmonton's games industry.

items: Edmonton-based indie game studio latest to take blockbuster-making skills and get 'pretty risky'

blocks.text: He noted that several independent studios have formed over the years from former BioWare developers, building games that may stray significantly from its role-playing game blueprint but still have "the same really strong character development and storytelling."
"I can't understate how influential those franchises from BioWare were to the industry at large. It really, really had a big impact."
Hale hopes Bioware's IPs will live on
In the days after BioWare's closure, a trailer for the now-cancelled Mass Effect game was leaked online, reportedly by a former BioWare employee.

An image from a reportedly leaked trailer for an upcoming Mass Effect game from BioWare. The studio was closed down by its parent company Electronic Arts on Oct. 21 and the game was cancelled mid-development. (Dejahvoe Ivoe/YouTube)

After watching the trailer for the first time, Hale called it "gorgeous," and said she holds out hope that if EA has no plans for one of its other studios complete the game, that it might sell the IP and let another team finish the work.
"I think the fans would be overjoyed if that IP found a place to live that was just some small, little maverick place.... They would engender a great deal of good will," she said.
"So let that thing go, and let us, the community, play and let us do beautiful things with this story that is still wanting to be told."

articles.title: AI giant Anthropic files papers to sell shares to the public for 1st time
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers on Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever.

image.caption: Dario Amodei, CEO and co-founder of Anthropic, attends the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Jan. 23, 2025. (Markus Schreiber/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business·New
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers on Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever.
Anthropic could be the biggest-ever initial public sale of stock, raising as much as $100B US, reports say

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers on Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever, even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86 billion US. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public in what is expected to be a pair of blockbuster stock debuts for the rival AI labs.
The filing comes weeks after CEO Dario Amodei argued in an essay for slowing the development of the most advanced AI models.

An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price, but even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world's most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela, by billions of dollars.

The 335-page document showed Anthropic's revenue is growing rapidly, but like many other tech companies going public, it has yet to turn a profit. The company behind the chatbot Claude reported a net loss of $80.7 billion US in the first half of 2026. That compares to a loss of $13 billion US in the same period a year earlier.
Why Nova Scotia's AI data centre feels like a surprise reveal

Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion US by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion US, Anthropic would rank among the world's most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla.
As for money raised, the offering could raise as much as $100 billion US, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by another one of Musk's companies, SpaceX, earlier this year.
In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT."

articles.title: US Marine indicted for murder and robbery of woman in Japan
articles.summary: Prosecutors have indicted Devin Jacob Ballard for a killing that has caused outrage in Japan, local media reports.

blocks.text: A US Marine has been indicted on suspicion of murdering and robbing a woman in Japan earlier this month in a case that has triggered protests, Japanese media reports.
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who was stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested on suspicion of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa.
Prosecutors have now indicted him for allegedly strangling Yagi with a telephone cord and then stealing her backpack and wallet on 3 October, media reports, citing the indictment document.
It wasreported Ballard had denied the allegations, but Asahi Shimbun and Kyodo News cited investigators saying he has made some statements suggesting involvement.
Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings.
Yagi's death has caused outrage in Japan, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi describing the crime as "brutal and heinous".

Earlier this month, the Marine Corps said it was "actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine" and extended condolences to the victim's family.
It is the latest case involving a US serviceman in Okinawa, which hosts the highest concentration of around 55,000 US soldiers stationed in Japan.

Previous criminal cases have sparked anger and protests, the largest of which took place in 1995, when tens of thousands took to the streets following the abduction, beating and rape of a 12-year-old girl.

In 2024 alone, there were four sexual assault cases involving US troops in Okinawa, including that of air force member Brennon Washington, who was given five years for the rape and kidnapping of an underage girl.
In 2025, US marine Lance Cpl Jamel Clayton was sentenced to seven years in prison for sexually assaulting a woman.
Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said the prefecture has repeatedly demanded that the US take action to prevent such incidents, and said he sees the alleged crime as a sign of a lack of discipline.

The prime minister said her government has registered a "strong" protest with the US and called for "strict disciplinary action against US military personnel and thorough measures to prevent a recurrence of such incidents".

People in Japan have been voicing anger, with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo earlier this month. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice, with one user saying: "Enough is enough."

articles.title: High-level delegation in Iran in push to avert flare-up of conflict with US
articles.summary:
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey travel to Tehran as bellicose rhetoric heightens

High-level diplomatic delegations from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have…

blocks.text: High-level diplomatic delegations from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have travelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent renewed fighting between Iran and the US and Israel as rhetoric sharpens on both sides.

Security officials and diplomats at Monday’s meeting were expected to discuss how Iran could persuade the Houthis in Yemen to end their crippling missile and drone attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. With fighting raging across Yemen, the Houthis claimed to have closed Riyadh airport and inflicted heavy damage on the Saudi economy.
The officials were also understood to be discussing Iran’s possible inclusion in a new security pact involving Islamic countries.

The Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and the head of Turkey’s intelligence service, Ibrahim Kalın, were to meet Iran’s top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington.

The three countries signed a defence agreement in Mecca in August. Some in Iran feared the deal was constructed to challenge Tehran, but the signatory countries have insisted it is simply a mutual defence pact.

The balance between exploring a new long-term security architecture and demanding Iran start to compromise in the conflicts in which it is engaged will be critical. It is possible the two sides came to the meeting with different priorities.

blocks.caption: The Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, meeting Pakistan’s Field Marshal Asim Munir in Riyadh in September.  Photograph: Saudi Press Agency/Reuters

blocks.text: The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role, and the US-Iran conflict has potentially reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran.

No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attack on Iran either last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said the meeting could pave the way for broader regional cooperation on security based on shared interest.

“The events of the last two years, especially the past eight months, have shown that sustainable and reliable security in our region will only be possible by building trust and cooperation among the countries of the region,” he said.

Javad Zarif, a former foreign minister and long-term advocate of a regional security alliance called for “a comprehensive regional network based on non-aggression, mutual trust building, and shared prosperity”.
“Regional security is not imported, it must be created by the people of this very region together,” he said.

He published his message alongside an image of verses 103 and 159 from Surah Ali ‘Imran, the third chapter of the Qur’an. The verses emphasise being saved from a fiery pit by avoiding division, fostering unity, seeking forgiveness and consulting others.

The meeting takes place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators, it was confirmed, spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz.
Israeli media reports claimed the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been trying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iran before the Israeli elections on Tuesday.
Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that modern-day US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity in the region.

The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners also increasingly argue Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb, ending the fatwa on the possession of a weapon of mass destruction.
A pact likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted.

articles.title: HIV infections among young people expected to increase by 2030, says AIDS society
articles.summary: By the year 2030, more young people aged 15 to 24 are projected to be diagnosed with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), the AIDS Society of the Philippines (ASP) reported Monday.

blocks.text: By the year 2030, more young people aged 15 to 24 are projected to be diagnosed with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), the AIDS Society of the Philippines (ASP) reported Monday.

“Let’s look at our young people kasi they are now getting infected… The estimate is that by 2030, which is above four years from now, I just don’t know baka nagbago ‘to, baka tumaas pa ‘yan. Makikita ninyo that we are estimating that the majority of our infections will be among the young people,” ASP President Dr. Rossana Ditangco said.

(Let’s look at our young people because they are now getting infected… The estimate is that by 2030, which is around four years from now—though I don’t know, this might change or go even higher—you will see that we are estimating that the majority of our infections will be among young people.)
“... Talagang magpe-predominate na siya. Paakyat nang paakyat and mostly young people, if wala talaga tayong ginagawa,” she added.
(... It will really become predominant. The numbers are continuously rising, mostly among the youth, if we do not take action.)
In the projected data presented by ASP, around 47,029 HIV cases by 2030 would belong to the 15 to 24 age group, while 17,446 would come from those aged 25 to 30.
Delayed access to services

According to Ditangco, a 2015 study by the Department of Health (DOH) found that risky behaviors among individuals in their sexual activities start early, but access to services remains delayed, putting young people at greater risk of contracting HIV and other sexually transmitted infections.

“How about the female sex workers? The first sex is at age 17. First paid sex and first condom use, age 20. Again, there’s a delay. So in between, nahahawa na sila or nakakapanghawa na sila, di ba?” Ditangco explained.

(How about female sex workers? Their first sexual encounter occurs at age 17, while their first paid sex and initial condom use happen at age 20. Once again, there is a delay, during which they can contract or transmit infections.)

“Ito namang mga MSM [men having sex with men], first sex and first anal sex… 16 at 17 years old pero ang first condom use ay 18 [years old]. So may delay. So in between that, pwede nang mahawa,” she added.

(As for men who have sex with men, their first sexual experience and first anal intercourse occur at ages 16 and 17, but their first condom use is at age 18. Because of this gap, transmission can already occur.)

Ditangco urged the public, especially government agencies and stakeholders, to provide young individuals with proper sex education and encourage responsible participation in sexual activities before they become sexually active.
The ASP said data show that among the general population of young males and females, only 17% have comprehensive knowledge about HIV.

“Studies have shown that people who use condoms consistently are the ones who used it during their sexual debut kasi they don’t know na the difference. Kasi ‘pag nag-umpisa ka ng sex nang walang condom at pinag-condom ka, parang hindi mo na gusto,” Ditangco said.

(Studies show that consistent condom users are those who used them during their first sexual experience, as it sets the baseline. If one begins having sex without a condom, introducing it later becomes much harder.)

“... So dapat talaga ‘yung pagse-sexual debut may condom na para talagang masanay silang gumamit ng condom subsequently. Ang condom pa naman napakaimportanteng intervention niyan for safety,” she added.
(... Condom use should ideally begin at sexual debut to build a consistent habit. Condoms remain an indispensable safety intervention.)
Further showing the disparity in access to services, the ASP noted that young MSM aged 15 to 17 face similar risks as older MSM, yet they have less access to condoms.
Destigmatizing, holistic approach
While a lack of condom access contributes to the growing number of HIV cases among young people, the ASP stressed that it is not the root cause of the country's HIV epidemic.

According to Ryan Pinili, a DOH-certified trainer in HIV Counseling and Testing, stigma and misconceptions heavily hinder efforts to raise awareness about HIV and assist people living with the virus in seeking treatment and support.

“We have to destigmatize kasi meron pa rin po tayong pananaw na pag nag-avail ng condom, nag-avail ng PrEP—kakanood lang po namin kanina, meron pong isang sikat na personalidad… mayroon po siyang masamang pagtingin sa PrEP and PEP, ang kailangan daw ituro ay abstinence.But the choice is nasa tao po,” Pinili said.

(We have to destigmatize because we still have that perspective that when you avail of condoms or avail of PrEP—we were just watching earlier, there is a famous personality… they have a bad view of PrEP and PEP, saying what should be taught is abstinence. But the choice is with the person.)
“... We have to destigmatize at kailangan sabihin natin kung saan po makakakuha ng readily-available na commodities. Libre naman po itong pinamimigay ng ating gobyerno,” he added.
(.. We have to destigmatize and make sure to inform people where they can get readily available commodities. These are distributed by our government for free.)
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a pill or injection that can reduce the chances of getting HIV, or stop the spread of HIV in the body once a person is exposed.
Meanwhile, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is taken within 72 hours by an HIV-negative person who has been or may have been exposed to HIV to reduce the risk of HIV transmission.
Pinili reminded the public that when a person living with HIV undergoes treatment and is declared to have an undetectable viral load, they are unable to transmit the virus to their sexual partners.
In an appeal to agencies and institutions, Ditangco emphasized the importance of adopting a holistic approach to HIV prevention and treatment in the country.

“Kaya nga ang ating prevention strategy must be a combination. Hindi pwedeng biomedical lang, na condom lang, PrEP and ARV. Dapat holistic— you address the emotional, the psychological, the social issues at different ages. Kasi pine-prepare mo na 'yung tao to behave responsibly,” Ditangco said.

(That’s why our prevention strategy must be a combination. It cannot be purely biomedical, relying solely on condoms, PrEP, and ARVs. It must be holistic—you need to address emotional, psychological, and social issues across different ages. That is how you prepare a person to behave responsibly.)
HIV epidemic
At present, the ASP noted that HIV in the Philippines can be considered an epidemic due to the increasing case counts and the rapid increase in data in recent years.
From January to March 2026, the Philippines logged 4,367 diagnosed HIV cases.

Data show that sexual contact remains the primary mode of transmission during the first quarter of 2026, with male-to-male contact accounting for the highest number of cases at 3,095, followed by contact with both male and female partners at 567.
Meanwhile, male-to-female sexual contact recorded 331 cases among males and 221 among females.
The ASP added that the occurrence of mother-to-child transmission is particularly concerning, with nine male and four female cases reported.
Ditangco emphasized that the DOH maintains zero tolerance for mother-to-child transmission, reiterating its call for universal testing among pregnant women.
Cases involving the sharing of infected needles were also recorded, with one case each reported for males and females. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: First Thing: Brazil re-elects Lula in comeback rebuke for Bolsonaro and far right
articles.summary:
Leftwing incumbent becomes first candidate to reverse first-round defeat, but far-right son of former president rejects result. Plus, interviews with two legendary songwriters

Good morning.…

blocks.text: Good morning. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has staged a dramatic election fightback, defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term as Brazil’s president. Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and asked for the results to be annulled.

Following in the footsteps of his father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who four years ago also refused to acknowledge his defeat to Lula – before attempting a coup and being convicted for it – Flávio Bolsonaro cited a supreme court justice’s decision to extend voting hours as the alleged reason for wanting to cancel the result.

items: What does this result mean for Brazil now? My colleagues Libby Brooks in London and Tom Phillips and São Paulo spoke overnight. Phillips said: “The Bolsonaro response is exactly as I feared, but I don’t think it will mean very much. All these world leaders are now recognising Lula’s win, and I don’t think Bolsonaro has a hope of overturning this result. [For Lula] this is the crescendo of an incredible, if sometimes controversial, 50-year political career. The first elected working-class leader of Brazil, who has helped millions of people escape poverty.”
You can find the full results of the election here, and our ongoing live coverage here.

blocks.text: ‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes

blocks.caption: Palestinians cross on foot past a military gate at an entrance to Hebron, which has been sealed off by Israeli forces. Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPA

blocks.text: With elections looming in Israel, Hebron in the occupied West Bank – a city of 250,000 people – has been sealed off by Israeli forces after Friday’s gun attack on a military checkpoint in which two Israeli soldiers were killed. The neighborhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of the attack, has been flattened.

The Hebron municipality said 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said the displaced population left voluntarily. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no vote in tomorrow’s elections, but their lives will be deeply affected by the outcome.

items: What has Hebron’s mayor said? Yousef al-Jabari accused the Israeli state of “collective punishment”, saying: “They have dragged people from their houses, and they have prevented the media from getting into the district … Netanyahu and his gang are using Palestinian land to displace Palestinian people, closing the city, closing the mosque, in order to achieve their political goals.”

How has a 21-year-old photographer described being the target of an Israeli attack? Zeinab Faraj found herself buried under rubble beside a dying colleague while reporting in Lebanon. “My heart stopped” as she heard a drone descending towards them, she said. “I’ve never heard anything like it in my life … It was terrifying.” The Israeli military later justified their attack, saying they had identified saboteurs violating the ceasefire. Human rights groups called it a war crime.

articles.title: Endangered turtles and ‘exceptional’ coral at risk from Woodside’s gas drilling in WA, watchdog says
articles.summary: Exclusive: EPA flags oil spill risk from proposed gasfield and threat to pygmy blue whales

blocks.text: Woodside Energy’s plan to drill for gas off Western Australia’s north-west coast could significantly damage “exceptional” coral reefs and it may be impossible to reduce the risk of an oil spill to an acceptable level, according to advice from the state’s independent environmental watchdog.

A draft letter from WA’s Environmental Protection Authority written in 2023, seen by the Guardian, sharply criticised Woodside’s proposal to develop the Browse gasfield, saying its plans to protect endangered turtles and blue whales near Scott Reef would be ineffective.

Woodside, Australia’s largest fossil fuel company, is hoping to win approval next year to develop the Browse basin, about 300km off the Kimberley coast. Scientists have warned it could damage the Scott Reef ecosystem, which is home to more than 1,500 species, many unique to the area.

EPA staff presented the draft letter to the authority’s board for approval in December 2023. In February 2024, two months after it was discussed, the EPA sent a letter to Woodside saying its preliminary view was to reject development of the vast gas reserve.

It was a significant setback to Woodside’s plan to drill more than 50 wells and pipe the gas 1,000km to its ageing North West Shelf gas export plant adjacent to the world heritage-listed Murujuga rock art.

The company won approval last year to run the North West Shelf until 2070. But it needs the gas from the Browse basin – Australia’s largest undeveloped source of gas – to feed it. If the processing plant was to operate until 2070 it could lead to about 88m tonnes of carbon dioxide being released into the atmosphere each year after the gas was burned.

blocks.caption: Scott Reef off the coast of Western Australia is home to more than 1,500 species. It sits over the underwater Browse gas basin. Photograph: Greenpeace

blocks.text: The concerns presented in the letter to the EPA board show the pressure on authorities to recommend against the gasfield development being approved. The development is being assessed by both the state and commonwealth EPAs. Ultimate decision-making power lies with environment ministers.

The letter shows the EPA board was advised by its staff that there was a threat of serious or irreversible harm to turtles and whales and more generally due to oil spills. The threats were considered serious enough that the staff said the precautionary principle should be invoked. It meant the EPA should assume the worst possible outcomes could occur.

In response to this near rejection of its proposal, Woodside added explosive-driven shear rams to its drilling plans, a step that could allow it to seal a leaking well in seconds. The company said this would reduce the “longest credible duration” of a “highly unlikely” well blowout, and potential oil spill, to about 12 hours.

Not all companies have faith in shear ram technology. In 2024, fellow WA gas exporter Chevron rejected “pyrotechnic shearing” technology for its own wells, describing it as unproven and impossible to test in the field.
A Woodside spokesperson said if the shear rams failed it would deploy a capping stack to stop the oil flow within 16 days.
But the EPA was advised in 2023 that if a well leaked for 13 days it was possible there could be “irreversible consequences” to Scott Reef.

The draft letter said Sandy Islet, a part of Scott Reef considered critical to the survival of endangered green turtles, would be threatened if the seabed subsided after Woodside extracted gas from beneath it. It said a proposal to top up the sand on the islet, where about 1,000 turtles breed each year, was a “high-risk” measure and its success was “likely to be limited”.

Woodside said it would address this by changing its plans so that no wells would be drilled within 20km of Sandy Islet. It also said the flaring of gas, which produces bright light that can confuse turtle’s navigation, would be restricted.
after newsletter promotion

The EPA board was also told noise, traffic and vessel strikes would have a significant impact on pygmy blue whales migrating between Timor and southern Australia. Scott Reef is the only known whale feeding ground on the migration route, according to the draft letter.

Woodside’s spokesperson said the company understood whales did feed at Scott Reef, but that this was opportunistic and the area was not as important as the ocean off Perth and other areas further south. Woodside agreed that Scott Reef and Sandy Islet had exceptional environmental value and it was important to protect them for future generations.

Glenn Walker, Greenpeace head of nature, said Woodside’s plans to address the concerns raised by the EPA did not go far enough and relied on “fanciful and unproven technology” to prevent a catastrophic oil spill.

“It would be a major backflip for both the WA EPA and the national EPA to now recommend approving this project,” he said. “It is now critical that these regulators maintain their independence from corporate and political influence and reject this destructive project.”
Greenpeace last week nominated Scott Reef for national heritage listing based on its ecological and scientific values.
Just two of the current nine-strong WA EPA board were in place when the watchdog told Woodside it was set to reject Browse.

One of those – the current chair, Darren Walsh – said in a statement the assessment had been lengthy because it was a complex project in a sensitive area. He said a final state report and recommendations on the proposal would be provided to the WA environment minister, Matthew Swinbourn, when it was complete. There would then be a three-week public appeal period before a decision was made.

A spokesperson for the national EPA said the development was being assessed under the national Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, and the “decision clock” had been paused while the agency waited on “further technical advice”.

Issues that have to be considered under national law include the potential impact on pygmy blue whales, green turtles, the marine environment in commonwealth waters and Murujuga rock art near the gas processing facility.

articles.title: The chaos in France is a ‘warning signal’ for Australia’s public spending and rising costs
articles.summary:
Australia’s public debt may be well below that of France but there are lessons to be taken from its economic woes

  • Get our

blocks.text: The explosion of discontent that led to major protests and violence in France and across Europe is a “warning signal” that Australia could follow the same path without an “honest conversation” about the budget, economists say.

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday to protest underfunded schools, as complaints of insufficient teacher numbers and dilapidated infrastructure mingled with broader discontent about cost-of-living pressures.
Here, and across the developed world, people are struggling to cope with the affordability crisis, as households grapple with high and rising prices.
The scale of the challenges in individual countries may be of a different order of magnitude, but the grievances are common.

Luke Hartigan, a senior economics lecturer at the University of Sydney, said it was clear there was no single factor behind the discontent in France, but soaring energy costs were having a major impact.
Fuel prices are up 36% this year in France, or three times the increase in Australia. The US-Israel war on Iran has sent European gas prices soaring as the northern hemisphere approaches winter.
More fundamental, however, is that France’s finances are buckling under its generous welfare state.

France’s high public debt, stagnant economy, and universal social security benefits have created a “binary” situation, Hartigan said, where citizens’ demands for better services and cost-of-living help are clashing with the country’s increasingly dire fiscal position.
France has not balanced its budget since 1974. Meanwhile, total public debt as a share of the economy has swelled to nearly 120%, according to the International Monetary Fund.
Australia’s total government debt pile looks benign in comparison at 53%. But a decade ago our debt was 40% of GDP, and a decade before that it was just under 10%.
Hartigan said France’s lacklustre economy had compounded its fiscal problems, underlining how Australia needed to work hard to boost productivity.
“If you think about trajectories, they [France’s challenges] give us an idea of where we could potentially be if we continue down this path,” Hartigan said.
“It’s a warning signal.”

Bob Breunig, the director of the ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, said there was a growing gap between what voters believed the government should be able to do, and what politicians were able to deliver.

“One thing that is happening everywhere is this narrative that the government should be able to solve all your problems, and that narrative has probably been pushed further in Europe than it has here. It’s failing in both places, but it’s pointier there than here,” Breunig said.
The evidence of this growing demand for government intervention is that French public spending now accounts for 58% of the economy, the IMF data shows.

In contrast, Australia’s total public spending is equivalent to 40% of our national output – the highest in data stretching back to 1990, outside the pandemic, and at similar levels to the United States and the United Kingdom.
after newsletter promotion
“All these protesters are asking the government to help them out, but the government has maxxed out the credit card,” Breunig said, who said France’s debt was “reaching levels that are unmanageable”.
“The federal government here can still borrow and has a lot of flexibility, and the French just have no money.”
President Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power has been marked with failed attempts to rein in spending.
“There’s a real sense that people don’t know what to do,” Breunig said.
The bond market reflects growing alarm with France’s fiscal trajectory.

France typically has to pay a higher interest rate on its 10-year debt than fiscally prudent Germany, and the gap between the two rates is a measure of financial markets’ confidence in France’s fiscal position.
That gap is now at its widest since the European debt crisis in 2011.

Amid structural pressures on the budget from an ageing population, the NDIS, higher interest rates, and the push for greater spending on national defence, Breunig agreed there were lessons for Australia in not allowing the country to drift too far and for too long.

“We need an honest public conversation about what the government can be expected to do and what it can’t, and then a conversation about how much that would cost and whether we are willing to pay for that.”

While the opposition has attacked what it sees as the deadening effect of high government spending on economic dynamism, Breunig said he was broadly “agnostic” whether repairing the budget involved lower spending or higher taxes.
“At the end of the day, making these decisions is exactly what democracy is for.”

articles.title: AI giant Anthropic unveils plans for blockbuster share listing
articles.summary: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
articles.byline: Kali Hays, Rachel Clun, Liv McMahon

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic has revealed details of its business ahead of its plans to sell shares to the public in what will likely be the largest stock market debut in history.
The company behind AI chatbot Claude revealed losses of more than $80.7bn (£60.5bn) in the first half of the year. It said it generated revenue of $16.3bn over the same period.
The number of shares to be released and their price range is yet to be determined.
Anthropic's valuation when it goes public has been expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which this summer was the biggest-ever stock listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion.
Anthropic said it will often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".
"In order to fully capture the opportunity in front of us, we need to invest more aggressively than would a business that operates in a more slowly changing technological regime," the firm said.
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets."
Anthropic said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT. It will be the first true AI company to go public, marking a test for the future of the technology.

Tech companies have been heavily investing in costly AI infrastructure and tools, like data centres and the informational models that underly all AI technology, pouring more than $1tn into the efforts over the last year alone.
Anthropic, which was founded just five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, announced its intention to go public in June.

Its most significant rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit, saying it, too, intended to go public. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

After the companies had decided on such plans, a wave of cyber-security and other types of technological breaches occurred involving their AI agents, or AI bots that are designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also gained public attention with new warnings that AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect the whole of humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

articles.title: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback
articles.summary: The left-wing incumbent president had lost the first round to right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.

blocks.text: Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.
Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since the return to civilian rule in 1985 to win an election after losing the first round of voting.
Lula told celebratory crowds this election is a "loss for negativity, lies", later adding "long live democracy".
Flávio Bolsonaro, who is the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled, which experts say is unlikely.
In an unprecedented move, polls were also extended for two hours on Sunday evening after both candidates made requests for different reasons.

Lula's team had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Senator Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as the reason for their request.
The decision - issued by the Supreme Court just as polling stations were due to close - meant that some had already shut and were not able to re-open.

Supreme Court President Kassio Nunes Marques - appointed by the older Bolsonaro - confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voting extension did not cause issues for the count or the electoral process.
Lula secured 51.79% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.21% - a difference of 4.4 million votes between the two candidates.
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.
His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030.
But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump.

Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" - which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard".

Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support.
Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.
While Trump has yet to react, other world leaders have been congratulating Lula on his win.
Ecuador President Daniel Noboa Azin said the region had "common enemies, shared challenges, and much to gain when we work together."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "democracy and multilateralism" had won. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez - also a left-wing leader - called it a "great victory", saying "the comeback of global progressivism has just begun". French President Emmanuel Macron said the two nations should work "in service of a more just world".
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called Lula's victory one for the "global south and progressive forces throughout the world".
Additional reporting by Vinícius de S. Mendes, BBC Brasil
