articles.title: Sudan paramilitary drone strikes cause mass power cuts in eastern states
articles.summary:
Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese army

Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five…

blocks.text: Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.

The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref, and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.
All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has been at war with the RSF, its former ally, since April 2023.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people who are already facing the world’s largest hunger crisis.
Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao, in Gedaref, said the power had been out there since early morning.
“My son is diabetic, his insulin has to be stored in the fridge,” he said over the phone, adding that he was scared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoiled.
“We have no idea when the power will come back,” he said.
Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams.
Sudan’s war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October, drone strikes killed more than 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.
Africa’s third-largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.
The majority of Sudan’s hospitals have been forced to close, at least 8 million children are out of school and swathes of the country cannot access basic services.

Abdelhafez Daafallah, a 54-year-old farmer, said over the phone from Al-Jazira’s Al-Junaid town: “The electricity had just started to improve three months ago, the power station the militia had destroyed was just repaired and we had hope our irrigation pumps would finally start running again.
“We hoped we would be able to finally get back to farming, but now the station has been hit,” he said, frustrated after nearly four years unable to work his land.
Farmers in Al-Jazira have struggled to rehabilitate and replant their land since the army recaptured the state from the RSF last year.
Further east, in Gedaref, Ibrahim Mohammed, 37, a grocer, said he was “already facing power cuts for hours before the strike”.
“Now I have chicken in the fridge, we either lose our entire stock, or will be forced to sell it off at any price, which is still a loss.”
Sudan is also grappling with unprecedented inflation and a currency that lost more than 25% of its value in recent weeks.

articles.title: NBI seeks transfer of Paolo Duterte's cyber libel complaint from Davao City
articles.summary: NBI Director Melvin Matibag said he will ask Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida for the transfer of the venue of the complaint from Davao to the DOJ-National Prosecution Service.

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 5:54pm

National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag on Monday said he will file a motion to have the Davao City prosecutor’s office inhibited from handling the libel and cyber libel complaints filed by Davao Representative Paolo Duterte.
Matibag said he will also ask Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida for the transfer of the venue of the complaint from Davao to the DOJ-National Prosecution Service.
“For what reason? We found out that the City Prosecutor, Prosecutor [Jhopee] Avanceña, is [the] first cousin of Ms. Honeylet Avanceña,” he said in a briefing.
Honeylet Avanceña is the partner of former president Rodrigo Duterte, the congressman's fafther.

“Alam naman natin sabihin walang legal relationship because by affinity wala naman, dahil hindi naman kasal, but still it develops a sense of alarming reason for us to transfer dahil nandodoon pa rin ‘yung malalim na relationship. To remove the bias,” he added.

(We know that we can say there is no legal relationship by affinity because they [Rodrigo Duterte and Honeylet Avanceña] are not married, but it still gives us cause for concern and a reason to transfer because that deep relationship is still there. To remove the bias.)
Last week, Congressman Duterte filed a libel and cyberlibel complaint against Matibag, dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., and GMA Network executives and journalists.

This stemmed from Gracioso’s allegation that he delivered suitcases containing cash to Paolo Duterte, Vice President Sara Duterte, and former president Rodrigo Duterte on the instruction of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
They have denied the allegations.
Matibag said Vida may also appoint a special prosecutor for the complaint.
“It’s the discretion of the Secretary of Justice, probably can appoint a special prosecutor for this purpose,” he said.
Sought for comment, Prosecutor General Richard Fadullon said this is up to the Justice Secretary’s discretion.

“It really depends on what the grounds are that are being relied on for the transfer kasi we do not see any reason why the other offices of the department where the office, which has jurisdiction… cannot take cognizance of the case,” he said.

“They will have to provide us with justifications as to why it cannot be heard there or why it’s not feasible to conduct the hearing there before it can be transferred here and that is a matter that the secretary of justice will have to act on,” he added. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults
articles.summary:
Faced with a stagnant jobs market, many are spurning children or pets in favour of ‘raising bricks’

Chinese young adults looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having pets or…

blocks.text: Chinese young adults looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having pets or children have found an answer: raising bricks.

Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media.

Raising “brick babies” is easier than house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day and waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article praised the bricks as being “practically immortal”: “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.”
A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on Weibo, a Chinese social media platform.

blocks.caption: Social media user documents their brick’s changes over a year, with hashtags including  #healingand #stress relief. Photograph: @South / xiaohongshu.com

blocks.text: Chinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick parent told Chinese media that the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”.

One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick baby, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”.
Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick.”

“A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.”

Chinese young people are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society such as having children and grinding out long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- 24-year-olds, excluding students, are unemployed, according to official statistics. Some estimates put the employment rate much higher.

China’s birthrate is in stubborn decline and fell to a record low last year. Faced with a sluggish job market after years of studying in an intensely competitive educational environment, many young people are choosing to drop out of the rat race, and opting instead for “lying flat” – pursuing a low effort, low stress lifestyle, well-suited to raising bricks.
The trend of raising bricks has become so popular that Chinese media has started to warn about the health risks.

Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of suffering from itchy eyes and a runny nose. Xuedong Li, a retired moss professor from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged brick parents to raise their mossy babies in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media.
Additional research by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: Brexit deal is not good enough for British public, says Andy Burnham
articles.summary: EU exit has damaged economy and failed to bring promised benefits, says PM, but he rules out big pre-election changes

blocks.text: Brexit has not “played out” like it was promised to the public, has weakened the economy and the current deal is not good enough, Andy Burnham has said, but he ruled out major changes in the current parliament.

The prime minister said Britain had ended up with a “harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign” and it had not helped to control the small boats crisis. Backing the home secretary’s tougher immigration rules, he said Brexit had weakened the UK’s ability to control its borders as it could no longer send people back to Europe.

When asked directly on Monday whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, Burnham told Good Morning Britain: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.”

Explaining why he even brought up the possibility of “going all the way” in terms of closer relations with the EU, Burnham said: “Looking back at Brexit … I don’t think it has played out as people said it would at the time. We got a harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign.

“It’s weakened our economy. It’s also weakened our control of immigration and that might surprise people because that was the big issue, but the small boats crisis has risen since and we have a different form of immigration now.”
He added: “I am not going to say at the moment that the deal we’ve got is good enough for Britain. I don’t think it is good enough.”

Burnham said he would not “move away from the red lines in Labour’s manifesto”, adding: “I’m not proposing rejoining [the EU] in this parliament. We’re way, way away from that at this particular point in time. What I am saying is we need to take some practical steps to make the arrangement work better.”
There are concerns among Labour MPs who represent leave voting constituencies in the north of the England and the Midlands that reopening the Brexit debate could create opportunities fro Reform UK.

On the fact that 65% of his constituents in Makerfield voted to leave the EU, the prime minister said: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’ doing. The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation to Brexit … What I can do though is make practical steps to make the arrangements work better.”

Emphasising the negative impact Brexit had had on Britain’s control of immigration, the Labour leader said: “I think we’ve got weaker control now. The reason the small boats crisis has arisen is because we can’t return people and people know we can’t do that in the same way that we used to be able to.”
The prime minister said he hoped the UK-EU summit on 20 November could yield a deal “which would be good for British food manufacturers because they’ve been hit hard by Brexit”.

He said he backed “the principle” of the home secretary’s controversial plan to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
Burnham said Shabana Mahmood was right to pursue the plans based on the principle that “settlement is a right to be earned not just something that is granted automatically”.

He also ruled out calling an early general election, despite polling suggesting Labour was still enjoying a “Burnham bounce”. “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.”

articles.title: BIR suspends controversial QR badge requirement
articles.summary: The BIR stops the mandatory online display of registration badges, which had an original deadline of October 31, following complaints over data privacy and additional red tape

blocks.text: The BIR stops the mandatory online display of registration badges, which had an original deadline of October 31, following complaints over data privacy and additional red tape

items: The Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) has suspended the requirement for online sellers and freelancers to display QR-coded tax registration badges due to privacy concerns and bureaucratic complications.

BIR Commissioner Charlito Martin Mendoza announced the suspension, stating that no penalties will be imposed for not displaying the badge during this period, and those who have it can choose to display it voluntarily.

Critics, including economist Cielo Magno, argue that the requirement added unnecessary burdens on small businesses and questioned its effectiveness in improving tax compliance, highlighting existing issues with the Philippines' complex business regulations.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Online sellers, freelancers, content creators, and other businesses no longer have to display QR-coded tax registration badges on their websites and social media pages after the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) suspended a controversial requirement that had drawn complaints over privacy risks and additional bureaucracy.
BIR Commissioner Charlito Martin Mendoza announced on Monday, October 26, that the requirement would be suspended indefinitely, just five days before the supposed October 31 compliance deadline.
No penalties will be imposed solely for failing to display the badge during the suspension. Those who already have their badges may continue displaying them voluntarily.

The requirement was introduced in April as an alternative to displaying one’s full BIR Certificate of Registration (COR) online. The badge contains a QR code that customers can scan to verify whether an online seller or service provider is registered with the tax bureau.

But what was supposed to make registration verification easier has since sparked debate that QR codes could expose personal information. The rollout was also marred by technical difficulties and confusion over who needed to comply.
“We recognize that protecting personal information online presents different and more complex challenges than displaying a COR at a physical business establishment,” Mendoza said.
The BIR said it would work with the National Privacy Commission and consult affected taxpayers before deciding how to proceed.

Economist and former finance undersecretary Cielo Magno welcomed the suspension but questioned why the requirement was necessary in the first place. Magno pointed out that the BIR already maintains taxpayer registration records and has other mechanisms for monitoring transactions.
She argued that requiring another badge, without clear evidence that it would improve revenue collection, merely adds another administrative burden onto small online sellers and freelancers.
“Instead of encouraging people to enter the formal economy, we risk giving them more reasons to remain outside it,” she said.
Her criticism comes amid longstanding concerns over the Philippines’ complicated business regulations and excessive red tape.

In its latest Business Ready assessment, the World Bank found that Philippine business regulations scored nearly as well as Singapore’s on paper, but the country lagged considerably in implementation. Registering a foreign firm in the Philippines takes 76 days, compared with just one day in Singapore, according to the World Bank.

The international lender has also urged the government to simplify tax compliance, arguing that easier procedures can improve collection by reducing mistakes and encouraging taxpayers to comply voluntarily. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Serbia wakes up to new reality after student-led movement ousts Vučić – Europe live
articles.summary: Hopes raised for a reset in relations with EU and other partners following the defeat of authoritarian president

blocks.text: Morning opening: Serbia wakes up to new reality after Vučić

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

Serbia wakes up to a new reality this morning after a grassroots opposition movement led by students ousted the country’s former authoritarian president Aleksandar Vučić, raising hopes for a new opening in relations with the EU and other partners.

blocks.caption: Opposition supporters celebrate at the parliament building after Aleksandar Vučić, represented by the silhouette, conceded defeat in the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters

blocks.text: With 96.9% polling stations processed, the Student List has 52.6% of votes, well ahead of Vučić’s bloc at 39.22%.

The latest CeSID projection suggested the students will have 140 seats in the new parliament, well clear of the 126 required for majority, with 103 for Vucic’s bloc. No other party crossed the 3% threshold, with national minority parties taking the remaining seven seats.
We are likely to get more reactions to the vote today, with international observers set to present their preliminary report on the vote in the early afternoon.
I will also pick up the latest on the first round of the presidential vote in Bulgaria, which saw a record-low turnout of just 22%. The second round will be held this Sunday.

Elsewhere, I will be looking for updates from France and Italy after another rocky weekend of protests. French PM Sébastien Lecornu is going to meet with the student unions in the afternoon for what could be pivotal talks on the future of the demonstrations.

And E5 defence ministers – that’s France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and the UK – are meeting in Paris for discussions on Ukraine. Oh, and Slovakia’s foreign minister Juraj Blanár is in Moscow for energy talks with Russia.
It’s Monday, 26 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Venezuelan opposition leader Machado returns from exile
articles.summary: Nobel Peace Prize winner and popular Venezuelan political opposition figure Maria Corina Machado has returned after nearly a year away. She was greeted by thousands of cheering supporters in Caracas.

image.caption: María Corina Machado leaned out of the sunroof of the car and waved to her supporters upon her return to VenezuelaImage: Federico Parra/AFP

blocks.text: Venezuela's opposition leader Maria Corina Machado was greeted by thousands of cheering supporters in Caracas on Sunday after returning from nearly a year in exile.

Her supporters stood along highways, toll plazas and city streets waving Venezuelan flags and chanting slogans like "freedom" as Machado made her way in a convoy of cars and motorcycles to the capital, Caracas.
Wearing her trademark white T-shirt and blue jeans, she leaned out of the sunroof and shouted "this country is giving lessons to everyone" as her convoy entered the capital.

blocks.caption: Maria Corina Machado was see singing the national anthem at a church after returning to the countryImage: Vente Venezuela Press/REUTERS

blocks.text: In Guacara earlier, the AFP news agency reported seeing Machado singing the national anthem in a plaza packed with supporters, waving flags and cheering her return.
Why was Machado in exile?
Machado left Venezuela last December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize for her work in promoting democracy in autocratic Venezuela.
Facing arrest by the regime of former President Nicolas Maduro, she sought refuge in the Argentine embassy in Caracas and was smuggled out of the country with assistance from the United States.
At first she was unable to return for fear of detention by authorities.
After the US-led ouster and arrest of Maduro, she gave her Nobel medal to US President Donald Trump.
However, her inability to return to Venezuela for so long was partly due to the Trump administration.
Instead of backing Machado, Washington decided to support interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

Machado has said she faced travel restrictions and flight cancellations, partly due to Trump's worries that her presence in Venezuela could inflame tensions during a period of transition, and partly due to Rodriguez' interference.

articles.title: Video of man helping homeless couple should inspire compassion and change, building manager says
articles.summary: A heartwarming video that shows a Londoner stopping to give warmth to a sleeping homeless couple offers an example of kindness and a stark reminder that institutions need to do better, a local man…

blocks.text: London

A heartwarming video that shows a Londoner stopping to give warmth to a sleeping homeless couple offers an example of kindness and a stark reminder that institutions need to do better, a local man says.
The incident was caught on a security camera on Oct. 13
A heartwarming video showing a Londoner stopping to warm a sleeping homeless couple offers an example of kindness and a stark reminder that institutions need to do better, a local man says.

"We must remember that these are human beings. They are people who deserve dignity, compassion and respect," said Muhammed Sajjad, the property manager for 734 Richmond St., where the video was filmed.
The 11-second video was sent to CBC News by building owner Umar Khan to commend the stranger's selfless act.
Filmed Oct. 13 at 6 a.m., the video shows a couple sleeping cuddled up on a dirty floor outside the upper level of an empty storefront.

A man in a red sweatshirt walks up the stairs, puts two sweatshirts over the couple, and gives them four loving pats on the back. The couple does not wake up during the interaction, and the man in the red sweatshirt walks away.

items: What have mayor and council done to address homelessness, addiction and mental health?

blocks.text: "What touched me about the video was seeing the gentleman offer his piece of clothing for the people who were sleeping outside in the cold," said Sajjad.

"He did not have to stop. He could have simply walked past them, but instead he chose to help. The small act of kindness sends a powerful message that even when people are struggling, we should never lose our humanity."
Homelessness has been a growing concern for property owners downtown, along Richmond Row, and in other parts of the city, Sajjad said.
LISTEN | Election issue:
London Morning6:33Is London's homeless and addictions crisis being used as an election campaign prop?

"We cannot depend only on the individual acts of kindness," he said. "We have to solve the problem because this is a serious issue. As a community, we need to ask ourselves why so many people are living outside and what we can do to help them."
London has to invest in long-term, practical solutions such as safe and accessible shelters, affordable housing, and mental health and addiction support where needed, Sajjad said.

items: Homelessness on the rise in Ontario while province on track to spend less, report says

blocks.text: "We also need better coordination between the city's community organizations and other level of the government," he added. "I hope that whoever leads our city will make homelessness a serious priority and work to toward meaningful, measurable results."

As a property manager, Sajjad sees people sleeping and even setting up encampments near businesses with increasing regularity. Protecting public spaces, supporting local businesses, and treating people experiencing homelessness with dignity should not be mutually exclusive, he said.
"Homelessness is not just one person's problem or one building's problem. It's a community issue, and we all have a role to play in finding a solution."

articles.title: I would like to rejoin EU, says Burnham, but ‘British public are the bosses’ – UK politics live
articles.summary:
PM says talking about changing the relationship with the bloc would not be divisive but ‘can start to bring people together’

Good morning. Andy Burnham started budget week…

blocks.text: Good morning. Andy Burnham started budget week with an interview on ITV’s Good Morning Britain with Susanna Reid and Richard Madeley. There were plenty of decent lines in it, but some of his most intriguing comments were about Brexit. Yesterday opposition parties (and even in private some Labour MPs) were criticising the PM for saying in a Sunday Times interview that he would be willing to consider going into the next election proposing accepting EU free movement rules. This was treated as if it was a novel outrage – even though at Labour conference Burnham announced that rejoining the EU could end up as the best option to emerge from his proposed renegotiation of the Brexit settlement, which of course would automatically involve accepting free movement.

Neil Kinnock said recently he thought Burnham was determined to take Britain back in the EU, but in his interview this morning Burnham insisted that he was not dogmatic in that way. When Madeley asked him if he saw himself as someone “destined” to be the PM would take Britain back in, Burnham replied:
double quotation markHonestly, I don’t. I see it as my job to be pragmatic about the whole situation. Can I make it work better? Can I add growth to the British economy?
And when Reid asked him bluntly to be honest and say if he wanted the UK to rejoin, Burnham replied:

double quotation markI’ve said – I’m going to be honest – in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here. You have to make sure that the British public are the bosses here.
When it was put to him that he had broken a promise he made during the Makerfield byelection campaign not to reopen the Brexit referendum campaign, Burnham said that was not what he was doing.
He repeated the argument he made in his Labour conference speech – that it was worth revising the relationship with the EU because the current, post-Brexit settlement was not working.
But he also claimed that, rather than being divisive, this new debate could bring people together. Later in the interview, he returned to Brexit unprompted.

double quotation markAnd [to] go back to Brexit, by just talking about it in a more practical way, by being honest about it … that can start to bring people together who voted in different ways. The divides that we’ve lived through in the last decade really do need to end, and we need to pull people together … I’m trying to give the country a direction and there is no way I can do that without coming back to the relationship with Europe and saying, ‘Look, here are some options as to how we got this right.’
Not for the first time, Burnham categorically ruled out trying to rejoin the EU before the election.
And, on the timing of the election, Burnham also insisted that it would be “no time soon”. He went on:

double quotation markMy mind is not on that [an early election]. I don’t know if that is coming over here, but it genuinely is not on that. There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well just put that out of their mind.
I will post more from the interview soon.
Here is the agenda for the day.
Morning: Andy Burnham is on a visit in London ahead of attending a summit on rough sleeping in Downing Street.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
2pm: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, and Robert Jenrick, his Treasury spokesperson, hold a press conference to present what they call their “economic rescue plan”.
2.30pm: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Ridon calls out PNP for double standard in arrest of journalist Lustre
articles.summary: Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon on Monday called out the Philippine National Police (PNP) for an alleged double standard in the arrest of veteran journalist Philip Lustre when the police never…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 4:49pm

Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon on Monday called out the Philippine National Police (PNP) for an alleged double standard in the arrest of veteran journalist Philip Lustre when the police never attempted to arrest Vice President Sara Duterte on grave threat charges.

“With specific emphasis on the case of Philip Lustre, it basically also reflects as to the manner by which the PNP had been implementing various arrest orders on different personalities. The double standard of the non-arrest of the Vice President is clearly at play on the arrest of Philip Lustre,” Ridon said in a press conference.

The grave threat charges was filed by the Department of Justice against the Vice President over the latter’s supposed threat to kill President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr., his wife Liza Marcos, and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez.

“There are questions today as to why in-implement ho 'yung Philip Lustre arrest [while] back then, hindi inimplement iyong Sara Duterte arrest when in fact we are talking about the same available offenses over the weekend. The Philippine National Police should clarify today: Bakit po inaresto si Philip Lustre samantalang hindi po inaresto ang atin pong Pangalawang Pangulo?” Ridon said.
(Why was Lustre arrested while the Vice President was not.)

“We are talking about the bailable offense of libel and the bailable offense of grave threats. What is the distinction that the Philippine National Police had implemented on both of these case? The police should explain their actions to the journalists and the Filipino people, why arrest a journalist who is being of service to the nation,” he added.
GMA News Online reached out to Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla for comment on the matter and will publish it once available.
The PNP is under the supervision of the DILG.
When the warrant of arrest for grave threat charges was issued against the Vice President, Remulla said arresting Duterte on site will paint her as a victim. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: NAIA braces for 1.25M Undas travelers; Oct. 30 seen as busiest day
articles.summary: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) is preparing for an estimated 1.25 million passengers during the Undas travel period from Oct. 27 to Nov. 4, with airport authorities projecting Oct. 30 to…

blocks.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) is preparing for an estimated 1.25 million passengers during the Undas travel period from Oct. 27 to Nov. 4, with airport authorities projecting Oct. 30 to be the busiest day.

In a news release, New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC), the airport operator, said it expects passenger traffic during the nine-day period to increase by 1% from the 1.24 million recorded during the same period last year. About 149,000 travelers are expected to pass through the airport on Oct. 30 alone.
To manage the holiday rush, NNIC said it would deploy additional personnel, strengthen security and passenger assistance services, and maintain round-the-clock monitoring of airport operations.

A 24-hour command center at Terminal 2 will coordinate responses to disruptions and other operational concerns, with airport personnel working alongside airlines, ground handlers, transport providers and government agencies, NNIC said.

The preparations involve the Department of Transportation, Manila International Airport Authority, Office for Transportation Security, Philippine National Police-Aviation Security Group, Bureau of Immigration, Bureau of Customs, Bureau of Quarantine and other agencies handling airport security, passenger processing and border control.
Police patrols will be increased at terminal entrances, curbside areas and parking facilities, with K-9 units and tighter access controls also deployed.
Additional screening personnel and checkpoints will be activated during peak hours, while technical teams will reportedly be ready to address equipment failures.
Immigration, customs and quarantine counters will be adjusted according to passenger volume, with additional counters opened when needed to ease queues.
Public Assistance Desks will operate around the clock in the arrival and departure areas of Terminals 1, 2 and 3 to provide directions, travel information, medical assistance and other services.
Traffic, baggage and flight operations
NNIC will also coordinate with road authorities and deploy traffic marshals to manage heavier vehicle traffic around the airport.
Taxi and shuttle services will be adjusted during peak periods, while inter-terminal shuttles will be scheduled according to passenger demand, NNIC said.
Additional porters and baggage carts will be made available to help travelers with their luggage.

On the airside, airport personnel will coordinate aircraft parking arrangements to accommodate additional and unscheduled flights and minimize delays caused by limited aircraft stand availability. Medical, firefighting, safety, engineering and technical teams will remain on duty throughout the travel period.

The operator said its teams would closely monitor aircraft movements, baggage handling and congestion at terminal entrances, check-in counters and boarding gates. NNIC will work with airlines and ground handlers to address bottlenecks and flight disruptions.
New facilities, immigration e-gates
The airport is entering this year's Undas period with additional facilities and supposedly upgraded passenger processing systems following more than two years of modernization under NNIC.

Among the developments is the completion of 78 automated immigration e-gates at Terminals 1 and 3. The gates allow eligible passengers to complete immigration processing in about 20 seconds, subject to Bureau of Immigration screening requirements.
Upgraded flight information displays, improved terminal access and waiting areas, and additional passenger facilities are also expected to support operations during the holiday period.
New restaurants, dining areas and lounges have likewise opened across the terminals, expanding the options available to passengers waiting for their flights.
Travel reminders

NNIC advised passengers to arrive at the airport at least three hours before international flights and two hours before domestic flights. Travelers should also verify their flight status and assigned terminal before leaving home and allow extra time for road traffic and security screening.
Passengers are encouraged to check in online when the service is available, prepare their travel documents in advance and observe baggage restrictions.

International travelers required to register through eTravel should complete the process within 72 hours before their scheduled arrival or departure. Registration is free through the official eTravel platform or the eGovPH app.
Passengers were also reminded to use authorized airport transport services and report illegal solicitors to airport personnel or police.
Those requiring assistance may approach the Public Assistance Desks at their respective terminals.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Reports show staffing shortages, training lapses and care failures in N.L. group homes
articles.summary: Group homes and residential care placements ensure children without a home have somewhere to live, and ideally, to thrive. A CBC News investigation has found that's not always the case.

image.caption: Annual compliance reports for group homes, emergency placement homes and independent living arrangements (ILAs) show strengths in supporting children and youth while addressing recurring operational deficiencies. (CBC News Graphics)

blocks.text: Vaden Johnson knows first hand that a good child and youth care worker can change a person’s life — and so can the wrong ones.
Having entered care at age 15, Johnson cycled through emergency placements, group homes, and independent living arrangements (ILAs).

While he recalls some dedicated workers who helped him learn to cook, drove him to school, and even helped move his furniture into his current apartment, he says that level of support was the exception rather than the rule.
"Drunken staff, no staff, people with little experience hired to just take care of people, locking themselves in the staff room while the kids lay waste," said Johnson, 20, of his first group home.
"I know the staff are doing the best they can, but choosing to put fresh new staff with disruptive people ends up shying them away [from the field]."
CBC News has obtained, through access to information, provincial government annual compliance reports for residential care providers.
They show a child and youth care system under strain, plagued by staffing shortages, systemic training lapses, and quality-of-care concerns.
At the same time, there was praise for staff who are "strong advocates" for children in their care, and homes that made gains in training and staff consistency.
The names of the private residential care providers are redacted from the documents provided to CBC News.

Leaders in the field say not all residential placements are the same, grappling with high staff turnover. And despite the concerns raised in those inspection reports, they say there has been much improvement over the years in child and youth care.
The challenges, they say, are complex and without easy answers.
Vaden Johnson says having a good child and youth care worker can make all the difference to a young person in care. (CBC)

Johnson says he eventually found his groove in the child protection system, building trust with residential placement managers and workers — though, he says, he hasn't had many stick around long-term.
It's been a rocky road to get to that point, punctuated by violence and uncertainly.

"There were kids trying to kill themselves with plastic spoons, like insane stuff. And the second home I lived in, it was that bad to the point where staff were constantly locking themselves in their own room because of violence and just people doing crazy stuff," Johnson said in a recent interview.

items: When it comes to aging out in N.L., the system is ‘leaving a lot of young people behind’

blocks.text: "I've had to personally go to staff and rat on my fellow group home people because I don't want to see people sniffing things or smoking crack or being high on pills."
Johnson believes child and youth care workers are underpaid, under stress, and often unprepared for the job.
"They've got 20-year-olds trying to take care of 18-year-olds," Johnson said.

The strain on child and youth care workers — and the subsequent repercussions for children in care — is a common thread through the annual reports obtained by CBC News, detailing performance reviews for service providers from 2023 through 2025.
Staff at one organization reported working 24-hour and 36-hour shifts, an annual report noted. In one extreme case, a worker completed a 60-hour shift.

"The overarching themes and concerns within these placements include staff training/qualifications, extended shifts contributing to staff stress and burnout and adherence to policy/protocols," the report said of four placements in the central-west region.

The documents also show some private operators are failing to ensure that front-line staff possess required training and qualifications, particularly regarding crisis management and trauma-informed care.

A lack of training at one service provider contributed to "inappropriate discipline, multiple referrals and investigations involving physical maltreatment, and gaps in staff knowledge related to responding to challenging behaviours," an annual report said.
Issues and accolades
An operator was found to have sweeping concerns over inadequate supervision, staff using cell phones on shift, staff sleeping while on duty, and staff using alcohol.

An investigation was launched at a different emergency placement home, in the St. John's metro area, after a young child began losing weight. The report says the weight loss was the result of "gaps in staff knowledge related to child development."
While there were serious issues flagged in the reports, there were also accolades for the workers and operators.
One annual report credits a group home with having "exceptional commitment to supporting the unique needs of children and youth in care."
The report commended the small operator for having Sunday suppers, where family members and friends are invited, and expanding garden space for outdoor activities.
Gordon Hawkins is president of the Child and Youth Care Association of Newfoundland and Labrador. (Ted Dillon/CBC)
Gordon Hawkins acknowledges the concerns raised in some of those reports, but says this province has a stellar reputation internationally when it comes to child and youth care.
Hawkins, president of the Child and Youth Care Association of Newfoundland and Labrador, says great strides have been made in the industry over the years.
"We are rather well-known for our child youth carers ... workers and our conferences and the community that we built," Hawkins said in a recent interview.
"But do we need more workers? Yes, we do. And, you know, some of the things in those reports are not good."
As of March, there were 225 children and youth in group homes, ILAs and emergency placement homes across Newfoundland and Labrador.
They are a necessary cog in the wheel of child protection, says Heather Modlin, who is a member of CYCA NL and is considered a longstanding leader in the field.
But they are also a costly one — nearly $112.5 million paid by the province to residential placement providers in the last fiscal year, according to records released through access to information.
That amount has nearly doubled in the past seven years.
How to find the best people for the job
Many of those in the child protection system carry heavy trauma, according to Modlin.

She says staff frequently manage intense, unpredictable, and sometimes frightening behaviours — physical aggression, severe emotional outbursts and self-harm — stemming from a child's past trauma and survival responses.

"It's highly unusual in regular life that you might be the recipient of some pretty significant insults — a shoe thrown at your head, a chair thrown at the wall, and [a threat] to slit your throat," Modlin said.
"You have to figure out how to manage that, recognize where it's coming from, not take it personally and then be the person to support the one who threw all that at you. And that's the job."
The debate around how — or if — the field of child and youth care should be regulated has been ongoing for years both nationally and internationally, she says.
The conversation has now shifted.
Industry leaders and a former teen in care give insights on the child and youth care system

"How do we ensure that children and youth and families who come to the attention of a child and youth care worker are going to receive competent care? That's the question," said Modlin, CEO of Amal Youth and Family Centre.
Amal, a non-profit that operates ILAs, group homes, and emergency placement homes across the province, has been steadily growing since 2021.
Employment standards and training rely heavily on employers rather than mandatory professional licensing. Modlin says it's incumbent on employers, like her, to ensure staff are prepared.
"Sometimes we get behind in training because things get in the way. But you can't lose the commitment to making sure that you do it," Modlin said.
"That's what we signed up for. If we're not going to be committed to providing the highest level of quality and keep working at that, then we shouldn't really be doing it."
Modlin believes there is good government oversight, and to make any drastic changes could create new problems.
"Like anything, things can always improve in some areas with organizations and government. But I do think we're in a very different place than we were even eight, nine years ago."
Increase in 'complex needs' cases, department says
Social Supports and Well-Being Minister Chris Tibbs declined an interview request.

In a statement, the department said it has oversight of staffed residential placements "through a comprehensive licensing, monitoring, and inspection process." That includes monthly visits by social workers.
The department acknowledged an increase in the number of children who have "multiple complex needs" and require specialized care.

"The department recognizes the increasing complexity of needs among some children and youth in care and continues to work with licensees to ensure appropriate staffing, training, and program quality across placements," the statement said.
The department said it's endeavouring to add more foster homes in the province, but adds that the complexity of some cases means there will always be a need for residential placements.

EDITOR'S NOTE: They are among society's most vulnerable: children who experience traumatic instability and end up in government care. In this series called "Left Behind," the CBC Atlantic investigative team explores the challenges and outcomes through the eyes of people who lived through this and those trying to help them.

articles.title: Alan Cayetano urges senators to reject offers for vice presidency if Sara Duterte is convicted
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano on Monday called on his fellow senators to declare that they will decline offers for the vice presidency should Vice President Sara Duterte get convicted in…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 4:22pm

Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano on Monday called on his fellow senators to declare that they will decline offers for the vice presidency should Vice President Sara Duterte get convicted in her impeachment trial.

Cayetano said this in a Facebook post in response to the statement of Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero that he will refuse the vice presidency, if Duterte gets convicted, due to conflict of interest as a senator-judge.
Escudero serves as presiding officer of the impeachment court in Duterte’s trial.
The Senate Minority Leader said that other senator-judges should make a similar commitment.
“Tama po ito! All of us senator-judges should make this declaration,” Cayetano said.

“It’s essential that in all impeachment proceedings (especially of Presidents and Vice Presidents), senator-judges are politically neutral and will have no incentive to convict except for evidence that proves the article/s of impeachment,” he added.
Uncalled for?
Senator Panfilo Lacson, however, said that Cayetano should not preempt the decision of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., should the vice president be convicted.
“Bakit niya pakikialaman ‘yung prerogative ng Pangulong pumili? Bakit niya lilimitahan? I think it’s uncalled for na pangunahan niya ‘yung Pangulo. Bahala ‘yung Pangulo pumili,” Lacson said.

(Why would he interfere with the President’s prerogative to choose? Why would he limit the President? I think it’s uncalled for for him to preempt the President. It should be up to the President to decide.)
“Paano kung, ang narinig ko medyo paborito si Senator Lito Lapid. Paano, ide-deny niya opportunity kung gusto ni Senator Lito? I don't think it’s proper,” he added.
(What if, I’ve heard that Senator Lito Lapid is a favorite? Would he deny Senator Lito the opportunity if he wants it? I don’t think that’s proper.)
Regardless, Lacson said he is not interested in the position as he intends to remain in the Senate until his term ends in 2031.
‘Too early’
Senator JV Ejercito, for his part, backed the call of Cayetano, but emphasized that it is too early to talk about the Vice President’s possible replacement as the impeachment trial is still ongoing.
“Maganda naman panawagan ni Senator Cayetano. Kaya lang, again, it's too early,” Ejercito said.
(Senator Cayetano’s call is well-intentioned. However, it’s too early to talk about that.)
“Hindi pa natin nasisigurado kung ano magiging verdict diba. Parang namang nakakasiguro na tayo. It's premature to talk about it,” he added.
(We don’t even know what the verdict will be yet, right? It’s as if we’re already certain about the outcome. It’s premature to talk about it.)

Malacañang earlier said that thoughts of a possible replacement for Duterte amid the ongoing impeachment trial is far from the President’s mind, and is not being discussed even during meetings. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Uganda imposes 21-day quarantine on citizens returning from DR Congo
articles.summary: Uganda will also not allow most travellers who have been in DR Congo to transit through the country.

blocks.text: Ugandans returning from neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, the health ministry has said, as the country tightens restrictions to contain the spread of Ebola virus.
More than 4,800 people have died in DR Congo since May - the country's deadliest outbreak of the disease - and has since spread to several other countries.
Uganda's restrictions follow questions after two people who had travelled through the country tested positive for Ebola, in Kenya and Nigeria.
The health ministry on Sunday said the 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan Ebola patient had all been discharged.
Announcing the new measures on Sunday, the health ministry said travellers who had been to DR Congo would not be allowed to transit through Uganda.
It said returning Ugandans would "undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost".
Uganda has also "intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings, supported by screening at designated road checkpoints", it added.
Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC's Newsday programme that only essential travellers from DR Congo would be allowed in but would be subjected to "intense public health measures".
"All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola," he said.

Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country free of the disease in August.
Concerns have however persisted after the two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day.

The patient in Nigeria is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya, while the Kenyan had travelled from the DR Congo where he had business interests.
Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients.
The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi, and the country has since confirmed eight other cases of Ebola. A second woman, related to the businessman died over the weekend.

Ugandan officials had previously said the patient in Nigeria had travelled to eastern DR Congo, only transiting through Uganda. On Sunday, however, the health ministry said Uganda and Nigeria were both working to establish her movements, complete travel history and possible routes of exposure.
The Ugandan health minister said the recent cases meant the risk had not ended and further underscored the need to "remain vigilant".
"We share a border with [DR Congo], where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties," Baryomunsi said.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind this outbreak is relatively rare and there is still no vaccine or specific treatment - though trials are under way.
Additional reporting by Swaibu Ibrahim in Kampala

articles.title: From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs — and why the connection is complicated
articles.summary: Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find…

image.caption: From rotten food and sexual behaviour to political beliefs, researchers want to know how different forms of disgust relate to our attitudesImage: picture alliance

blocks.text: Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.
One explanation begins with evolution.
"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.
What are the three types of disgust?
But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

items: Pathogen disgust: Reactions to potential sources of infection, such as rotten food, vomit or bodily waste.
Sexual disgust: Reactions to particular sexual behaviors or situations.
Moral disgust: Reactions to wrongdoing, such as betrayal or cruelty. Researchers debate whether this reflects physical revulsion or moral disapproval.

blocks.text: One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump used language evoking contagion when describing immigrants early in his 2024 presidential campaignImage: Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.
"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."
Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.
"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.
Do liberals and conservatives feel disgust differently?
Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.
A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in the US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.
However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.
Can our bodies reveal our politics?
Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.
Many US voters are undecided, disillusioned or disengaged
But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.
Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.
"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.
How do gut feelings influence political beliefs?
Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.
"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."
The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."
They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.
But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.
What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

blocks.caption: Pathogen disgust is one type of disgust thought to have evolved to protect us from infectionImage: Elena Shishkina/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: "People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.
Can disgust actually be measured?
Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.
He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.
Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.
"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.
The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.
Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."
How might politicians exploit feelings of disgust?
Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.
"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.
Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?
"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.
Does disgust influence how people vote?

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.
"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.
Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance.
"The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.
"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."
Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.
He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.
"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said.

articles.title: The Bank of Canada's inflation dilemma
articles.summary: Canada's economy is weak, but inflation is rising. The Bank of Canada has to choose which problem to take on. Raising interest rates will weaken the economy further while lowering rates would make…

image.caption: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem is seen during a news conference in Ottawa, on June 10, 2026. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business·Analysis

Canada's economy is weak, but inflation is rising. The Bank of Canada has to choose which problem to take on. Raising interest rates will weaken the economy further while lowering rates would make inflation worse. The central bank decides what to do on Wednesday.
Canada's economy has 2 key issues; the Bank of Canada can't fight both
This story is part of Mind Your Business, a weekly analysis of the biggest business stories emailed to subscribers on Monday mornings. If you haven't subscribed yet, you can do that by clicking here.
The Canadian economy is facing two very distinct problems right now.

On the one hand, inflation is high and rising. So far, at least, price increases have been contained to energy. Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent last month, but core measures (which strip out more volatile components) remained subdued.
But as we saw in the U.S., the containment doesn't hold forever — and once price increases spill over into other sectors, it can be tough to rein them back in.
On the other hand, the economy is weak. And we haven't even really started to get a measure of the impact of the latest tranche of tariffs.
Those two duelling crises pose a difficult riddle for the Bank of Canada.

Weak growth would usually prompt the central bank to cut interest rates to spur some economic growth. But rising inflation makes the bank want to raise rates to slow the economy and keep prices from increasing too quickly.
Two problems — with two solutions in complete contradiction to one another.
'We have to be realistic' about Canada-U.S. situation, Bank of Canada governor says
One by one, most of the major economic outfits in the country have switched their forecasts. Most now believe that on Wednesday the Bank of Canada will increase its key overnight lending rate.

They all lay out the economics of the matter, but as Frances Donald and Nathan Janzen from RBC Economics remind us, the bank is seeing this year's surge in inflation through the prism of the last surge — the pandemic shock of 2022 to 2023.

"The cautionary lessons of the post-pandemic inflation surge ... demonstrated how supply-side shocks and persistent cost pressures can overwhelm an economy surprisingly quickly," wrote Donald and Janzen in a note to clients last week.
So, most economists now believe the bank will increase rates, even though they don't all feel the bank should make such a move.

Donald and Janzen say a quarter-point increase won't materially move the needle on where they think the economy is headed. (They had, after all, built their forecast on the assumption that rates were going to rise next year.)

"Ultimately, the signal of a rate hike on Oct. 28 has a larger meaning we shouldn’t ignore: Central banks do not have the same patience for inflation they might have had in the past, and are willing to act pre-emptively to guard against it," they wrote.

items: Bond yields are soaring to multi-decade highs. What does that mean for Canadian consumers?

blocks.text: If we could wave a magic wand, we would probably like the economic data this week to come in opposite order. We have the interest rate decision on Wednesday and GDP numbers on Friday.

GDP stalled in July (zero per cent growth) and the economy is expected to have grown by 0.1 per cent in August. But new tariffs kicked in that month, so the risks to the forecast remain firmly planted on the downside.
Uncertainty is the new ... everything.
The Canadian economy and the Canadian consumer have both proven themselves to be far more resilient than expected. But each new obstacle takes a fresh swipe out of the Canada's potential growth.
On the upside, we will also get an update on the Bank of Canada's forecasts this week. The Monetary Policy Report is the central bank's deep dive into where it sees the economy headed.

items: Inflation risks rise with higher fuel costs and new U.S. tariffs, Bank of Canada governor warns
Inflation rises to 3.1% in September, as fuel prices push higher: StatsCan

blocks.text: ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Armstrong is the CBC's senior business correspondent. He was a foreign correspondent and a parliamentary reporter for CBC News. Peter hosted the business program On the Money and World Report on CBC Radio. He is the author of the CBC newsletter Mind Your Business

articles.title: A new cancer drug costs as much as a home down payment each month. Doctors say that's greed, not health care
articles.summary: Vancouver's James Howard is paying $90,000 a month for a new pancreatic cancer treatment that may add a few more months to his life. But, he's far from the only Canadian who is faced with having to…

image.caption: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the drug daraxonrasib to treat pancreatic cancer in August, but it's not yet approved in Canada. That means Canadian patients who want access to the medicine may have to pay tens of thousands of dollars out of pocket to access it. (Danielle Villasana/Re

blocks.text: James Howard thinks most people would say they're willing to pay any price to stay alive — until they're asked to put a dollar figure on it.
"The question that nobody's ever prepared to ask themselves is how much is your life worth ... and how long does that decision take for you," he said.
For Howard, the answer is $90,000 a month for a new pancreatic cancer drug he hopes will extend his life.
Doctors in Vancouver diagnosed Howard with pancreatic cancer in November 2025. He underwent chemotherapy, but the cancer has since metastasized and is now Stage 4.

Earlier this year, he learned about daraxonrasib, a treatment approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in August but not yet in Canada. At three doses a day, it costs him about $63,000 US — roughly $90,000 Cdn — a month.

Howard is far from the only Canadian confronting the soaring cost of new cancer treatments. Oncologists across the country say increasingly expensive drugs — particularly treatments not yet approved or publicly funded in Canada — are forcing some patients to choose between paying enormous sums themselves and going without potentially life-extending medication.

James Howard, seen in his Vancouver home, takes three doses per day of the new pancreatic cancer drug daraxonrasib, which isn't approved in Canada and that he has to get from the U.S. at a cost of about $90,000 Cdn. a month. (Glen Kugelstadt/CBC News)
More than two dozen cancer specialists who spoke with CBC News said the trend is putting growing pressure on patients and the public health-care system.
It's not that pharmaceutical companies don't deserve to make money from their products, says Dr. Christopher Booth, a medical oncologist in Kingston, Ont.
But he says prices have reached a point where profit can come at the expense of patients.
"Corporate greed is gonna harm patients and health systems," he said.

items: 'Game changer' experimental drug doubles survival time for pancreatic cancer, trial shows

blocks.text: An ecosystem that forbids negotiation

Booth, who is also a health-services researcher at Queen's University in Kingston, Ont., has been treating patients with pancreatic cancer — one of the most lethal forms of the disease — for more than 20 years.
He says U.S. drugs like daraxonrasib are approved and funded in an "ecosystem that essentially forbids" negotiation.
In Canada, Health Canada will give regulatory approval for doctors and hospitals to use a drug and then health authorities will work with the drug companies to determine a price.

items: A novel mRNA cancer vaccine helps cut the chances of melanoma tumor recurrence in major study

blocks.text: But in the U.S., he says, it's illegal for the government to negotiate with the pharmaceutical companies when they launch most new drugs — a rule that was eased slightly in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act — allowing the manufacturers to set their own price.

The median net price for new drugs launched in the U.S. was more than $250,000 US last year, according to a new report from the Boston-based Institute for Clinical and Economic Review (ICER), up more than 35 per cent from the $190,000 US median three years earlier.
California-based drug maker Revolution Medicines set its launch price for daraxonrasib at $480,000 US ($675,000 Cdn) annually, or $40,000 for a 30-day supply at wholesale cost.
Trump’s push to cut pharma costs could drive up drug prices in Canada
Profits over patients

Booth recalls how he and many of his colleagues were "thrilled" to see a treatment like daraxonrasib, a pill targeting a specific mutation in pancreatic cancer cells, prove effective in clinical trials.

The research found daraxonrasib halted or reversed tumour progression in nearly a third of patients, compared with about 10 per cent of those given chemotherapy, and increased survival from less than seven months to roughly 13.
"It was a signal of hope that we finally started to see some progress in this very difficult disease," Booth told CBC News.
But the excitement faded when Revolution Medicines announced the price of the drug, marketed as Rasonque.
LISTEN | Is Canada too reliant on the global supply chain for pharmaceuticals:
Cost of Living9:13Why is Canada so vulnerable to drug shortages?
In a statement emailed to CBC News, Revolution Medicines said how much a patient pays out of pocket depends on factors including treatment duration and insurance coverage.
"Our goal is to establish a price that reflects meaningful therapeutic advancement while supporting patient access and continued scientific innovation," a spokesperson wrote.
But doctors whose patients may benefit from daraxonrasib question the price.
"Sometimes the prices they quote make absolutely no sense," said Dr. Ramy Saleh, an associate professor of oncology at McGill University who researches early-stage clinical trials.

"I'm not convinced as an oncologist or a researcher that when a drug is approved that it will cost half a million a year, he said. "I'm pretty sure to produce it is, you know, a fraction of that cost."

A Revolution Medicines facility in Redwood City, Calif. The company developed daraxonrasib, a new pancreatic cancer drug that has been approved in the U.S. but not yet in Canada. (Revolution Medicines)
Dr. Ralph Wong, a senior medical oncologist at CancerCare Manitoba, accuses the company of profiting off the backs of patients like his.
"I've had multiple patients in my practice crying because they can't access the drug," he said.

items: Ontario cancer patients speak out over disappointment with drug funding decision
What Trump's 'most favoured nation' drug pricing policy might mean for Canadians

blocks.text: Wong says it's "particularly galling" that Revolution Medicines set such a high benchmark price based on its clinical-trial results rather than what he considers a price that would support patient access.
He and other doctors say they do everything they can to get patients free access through clinical trials or compassionate-access programs.
But if a drug isn't approved by Health Canada or covered by public or private insurance, patients can be left to pay for it themselves.
Revolution Medicines has yet to apply for Canadian approval of daraxonrasib.
Drug doubles survival time for pancreatic cancer patients, trial shows
'Crippling' cost of longer life
While wealthy patients may be able to manage the price of a drug like daraxonrasib, Booth said it would be financially "crippling" for many.
Data from the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board (PMBRB), the arms-length federal agency that regulates patented drug prices, show Canadians are spending more on medications.

Sales of patented drugs reached $22.1 billion in 2024, up nearly 11 percent in a year, according to the PMPRB's most recent annual report. Patented medicines accounted for 47 per cent of all spending on medicines. There were 1,137 patented medicines approved for human use in Canada that year.

items: Why millions of Canadian taxpayer dollars are spent on U.S. medical treatments

blocks.text: And that doesn't include what some patients pay for medications that aren't available in Canada.
For Howard, paying for daraxonrasib is like making a "down payment for a condo every month" for the hope of prolonging his life.
"It's not sustainable long term," he said, especially with all of the hurdles involved in getting the drug, including crossing the border to pick up the prescription at a U.S. postal address.
"[But] if I can gain a quality of life which allows you to spend more time with family, that's a significant bonus for me."
