articles.title: First Nations want tangible results as 'historic' first ministers' meeting opens
articles.summary: First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers will meet in Ottawa to discuss Indigenous rights for the first time in two decades, amid warnings and a planned protest against what the Assembly of…

image.caption: Assembly of First Nations chiefs and provincial premiers gather for a group photo at the AFN First Nations - First Ministers Meeting Day of Ceremony in Ottawa, on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (The Canadian Press/Keito Newman)

blocks.text: Indigenous·New

First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers will meet in Ottawa to discuss Indigenous rights for the first time in two decades, amid warnings and a planned protest against what the Assembly of First Nations is calling an "historic gathering."
Negotiations held all weekend to discuss potential outcomes, agreement
The warning 43 years ago was about good talk without action.

It's why Indigenous leaders approached prime minister Pierre Trudeau's 1983 first ministers conference on constitutional rights with caution — concerned about holding negotiations to hold more negotiations, and about skeptical premiers primed to listen but not understand.

On Monday, First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers will meet again in Ottawa to discuss Indigenous rights, the first such meeting in two decades, with those same warnings looming over what the Assembly of First Nations is calling an "historic gathering."

"First Nations and Canada and the provinces are at a crossroads," Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, national chief of the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) told CBC Indigenous. "Many chiefs have told us that they see this meeting as a chance to chart maybe a path forward, a new path forward."

At an AFN-organized ceremony on Sunday few would speculate on what the meeting's outcome will be, but for chiefs the mantra going in is "tangible results." They stressed it can't be a "one-and-done" event.

"We're a minority in our own country," said Kelsey Jacko, chief of Cold Lake First Nations in Alberta, "and everybody's living off the milk and honey of our lands, but we're being left out, so we need a seat at the table."
Indigenous leaders meet to amend the Canadian Constitution in 1982

AFN, a national advocacy organization, has circulated several discussion papers suggesting it might seek commitments on building economic prosperity, policing, constitutional rights, health and education.

Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty on Sunday declined to speculate on potential outcomes, saying the federal government's top priority is "to listen, to learn and to discuss how we can move forward."

The AFN also circulated among First Nations a draft of a "Declaration of a Shared Path Forward" to be considered at the meeting that, if agreed to, would commit the parties to continue these meetings on an annual basis.
"If this goes well, then maybe that's what's in the future," New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt told reporters walking into the ceremony on Sunday.

However Woodhouse Nepinak said Friday "you will not see a declaration" following the meeting because the AFN needs more time to consult its chiefs, with negotiations continuing on potential outcomes all weekend.
First such meeting since 2005
The last Indigenous-focused first ministers meeting was held in 2005 in Kelowna, B.C., seeking solutions to close the gap in living standards and yielding an agreement dubbed the Kelowna Accord.

To prepare for this meeting, Woodhouse Nepinak was thinking back to the 1983 Indigenous rights conference and its famous moments, beginning with Pierre Trudeau interrupting the chiefs' ceremonial opening prayer then answering it with prayer of his own, which she called "hard to watch."
Several premiers or their ministers attended the AFN's day of ceremony on Sunday. Prime Minister Mark Carney didn't attend but sent Alty in his place.
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak at the AFN's Day of Ceremony on Sunday. (Brett Forester/CBC News)
The closed-door meeting comes as fundamental issues of Indigenous land title, self-determination and place in confederation remain fractious.
In Alberta last week, First Nations celebrated the decisive defeat of a separation referendum called by Premier Danielle Smith. Quebec just elected a new sovereigntist Parti Québécois government.
The B.C. Conservative Party, which campaigned on repealing the province's legislation on the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, won a majority government on Saturday.
Federally, Carney proposed the meeting while facing backlash for his hyperfocus on fast-tracking development of major infrastructure and energy projects, pipelines in particular.
"Of course they want major projects," Woodhouse Nepinak reiterated,"but they're not going to get there without First Nations."

Speaking in French with Radio-Canada's Espaces autochtones, AFN's Quebec/Labrador Regional Chief Francis Verreault-Paul likened the situation facing First Nations to the one Canada faces, according to Carney, as a middle power on the world stage.
Verreault-Paul quoted Carney's headline-grabbing speech earlier this year in Davos, where he said,"if you are not at the table, you are on the menu."
“Right now, First Nations are not at the table for these major projects, " Verreault-Paul said.
Does that mean they're on the menu? Russ Diabo would probably say yes.
'Recipe for conflict'?
A member of the Mohawk Nation of Kahnawà:ke and a spokesperson for the Truth Before Reconciliation Network, Diabo helped organize a grassroots rally outside the meeting.
"We're challenging their mandate," he said, meaning AFN, "saying they don't have one to represent rights-holders, the inherent and treaty-rights holders."
AFN's national chief position is elected by chiefs and not popular vote among First Nations people. It also has no Alberta regional chief and sometimes faces questions about its relevance.
"It's a recipe for conflict, I think, because First Nations rights-holders weren't involved in this. It was just with chiefs — and select chiefs," Diabo said.

Three First Nations also raised those concerns in an open letter, warning about the meeting becoming "political cover" for the federal agenda. One signatory, Onion Lake Cree Nation on the Alberta-Saskatchewan border, also sent AFN a formal cease-and-desist notice.

"I'll be outside with the grassroots people," Onion Lake Chief Darwin Peter Chief said in an interview. "We're standing alongside First Nations in defence of our inherent treaty rights and independence and our right to determine our own future."

His community has serious and long-standing concerns about representation, transparency, meaningful consultation and the protection of treaty rights, he said, and wrote. Woodhouse Nepinak said she welcomes the peaceful protest.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Brett Forester is a senior reporter with CBC Indigenous in Ottawa. He is a member of the Chippewas of Kettle and Stony Point First Nation in southern Ontario who previously worked as a journalist with the Aboriginal Peoples Television Network.
With files from Radio-Canada's Dominique Degré

articles.title: Historic lawsuit challenging government over climate inaction begins trial hearings
articles.summary: After a seven year wait and a circuitous path through the justice system, a climate lawsuit against the federal government is finally getting its trial hearings this week in Vancouver.

image.caption: A fire this summer near Okanagan Lake in British Columbia. The youth applicants going to court this week are arguing that government inaction on climate change will violate their Charter rights. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Science
After a seven year wait and a circuitous path through the justice system, a climate lawsuit against the federal government is finally getting its trial hearings this week in Vancouver.
Youth plaintiffs are arguing in Vancouver that climate inaction violates their Charter rights
After a seven-year wait and a circuitous path through the justice system, a climate lawsuit against the federal government is finally getting its trial hearings this week in Vancouver.

The lawsuit, launched by 15 youth applicants who claim their Charter rights to life, liberty and security of the person have been violated because of the government’s inadequate action on fighting climate change, was first filed in 2019. It was initially dismissed by the Federal Court, then sent back for a full hearing by the Federal Court of Appeal.

items: Ottawa argues youth-led climate change lawsuit too broad to be tried in court
Youth activists say Canada has legal duty to protect vital resources as public hearing ends

blocks.text: It is the most prominent of several legal challenges based on climate policy across Canada, and has gotten further than any others. This is the first time such a lawsuit will receive a full hearing in court, with the potential for a precedent-setting judgment that could influence Canadian law and inspire other climate lawsuits around the world.
Nine of the 15 youth plaintiffs in the case in Vancouver when it was first filed in 2019. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
What do the applicants want?
The applicants want the court to declare that not doing enough on climate action is, in fact, a violation of Canadians’ rights.

Their key argument is that the federal government’s landmark climate law, the Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act, puts the country on an emissions trajectory that is inconsistent with a safe and livable future.

Essentially, the lawsuit argues that despite the government’s emissions targets and current policies to decarbonize, it still is not aligned with what scientists say is required to stave off the worst impacts of climate change.
“It's hard to see how our governments aren't taking the proper stand needed to combat this crisis because it seems so urgent to me,” said Sadie Vipond, one of the applicants in the case.

Vipond was seven years old when she remembers her grandmother waking her up in the middle of the night, telling her they needed to flee from rising waters during the 2013 Calgary floods. She was 13 when she joined the climate lawsuit, and has experienced many more climate-related disasters since then — wildfire smoke, extreme heat waves and a near-repeat of those Calgary floods. She’s now a student at the University of British Columbia studying environmental science.

As a remedy, Vipond and her fellow applicants want the government to develop a new climate plan that’s backed by the latest scientific evidence on avoiding climate impacts, and open to further judicial review to make sure it remains strong.
"I would like to see my country be able to take a stand for what I know is right," said Vipond.
How will the trial unfold?

The hearings begin on Monday, and the applicants and their expert witnesses will be testifying in the first two weeks. Vipond and other applicants will speak about the climate harms they have experienced — which have piled up in the past seven years as extreme heat, wildfires and flooding have touched the lives and millions of Canadians.

The applicants will have eight expert witnesses, including prominent climate scientists and experts in health, international law, clean energy and Indigenous rights. Two of their witnesses have been lead authors for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the premier global climate science agency that advises the UN.
The government is expected to present their side in the third week, with four witnesses who are experts in climate science, law and economics.

The government is not disputing that climate science is real and causing harm. But it is expected to argue that Canada's laws are not directly harming the youth plaintiffs, according to Columbia University's Sabin Center for Climate Change Law, which studies climate-related litigation worldwide.

A key legal debate in this case is whether Section 7 of the Charter, which guarantees life, liberty and security, imposes what's known as a "positive obligation" on the government. In other words: is the government constitutionally required to proactively protect Canadians from climate harms by enacting laws or other actions?

A court ruling on this question “would constitute a major development in Canadian constitutional law,” wrote human rights lawyer Catherine Savard, Canadian expert for the Sabin Center in New York City.
After the government witnesses, the hearings will take a break and both sides will return in February to make closing arguments.
The outcome will be closely watched around the world. The Canadian case is the first major climate trial since a landmark opinion from the International Court of Justice last year.

The global court found that countries could be in violation of international law if they didn’t take steps to reduce emissions, and countries that are suffering the impacts of climate disasters could seek compensation from the countries causing climate change.
“I think there is a very important role for the courts here in terms of protecting constitutional rights,” said David Wu, partner at the law firm Arvay Finlay who is representing the applicants.
“Are we going to allow governments to do what they want in terms of climate policy or targets or does our Constitution have something to say about it?”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Inayat Singh covers the environment and climate change at CBC News. He is based in Toronto and has previously reported from Winnipeg. Email: inayat.singh@cbc.ca

articles.title: NBI files cyberlibel, obstruction of justice referral vs. ex-Sara Duterte aide Jefry Tupas
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) on Monday filed a referral with the Department of Justice (DOJ) against former Davao City chief information officer Jefry Tupas.

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 3:59pm
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) on Monday filed a referral with the Department of Justice (DOJ) against former Davao City chief information officer Jefry Tupas.
The complaint was for cyberlibel, obstruction of justice, and publication of false news.

“We will be filing… a case of obstruction of justice, cyberlibel, and publication of false news under the Revised Penal Code will be filed against Jefry Tupas,” NBI Director Melvin Matibag said in a press briefing.
“So we’re endorsing it to the DOJ for proper disposition,” he added.
This stemmed from the sworn statement submitted by dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

Gracioso claimed that he delivered cash to Vice President Sara Duterte, former President Rodrigo Duterte, and Davao Representative Paolo Duterte on the instructions of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
He also claimed that Tupas received the cash on behalf of the Vice President.
Tupas has denied Gracioso’s claims and submitted his affidavit with the bureau. He alleged that NBI agents offered him cash and a place to stay in the upscale Forbes Park in Makati City.
The Tupas camp has yet to issue a statement.
Similarly, Sara Duterte, Paolo Duterte, and Velasco have submitted affidavits denying the allegations against them.
Paolo Duterte has also filed a cyberlibel complaint against Matibag, Gracioso as well as GMA Network executives and journalists. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in Party
articles.summary: The highly secretive four-day Plenum starts Monday in Beijing.

blocks.text: Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This years plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past Plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.

According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This Plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

articles.title: ‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes
articles.summary:
Families forced to flee as Netanyahu tries to prove security credentials after two Israeli soldiers killed days before election

Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little…
articles.byline: Julian Borger, Sufian Taha and Quique Kierszenbaum in Hebron

blocks.text: Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little attention to Israel’s looming elections until it found itself suddenly in the midst of them, a proving ground for Benjamin Netanyahu’s security credentials in the run-up to Tuesday’s vote.

A gun attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday in which two soldiers were killed brought immediate televised visits from Netanyahu and his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, whose ruling coalition is narrowly trailing with two days of campaigning left.
They vowed abrupt and sweeping retribution, and the prime minister warned of imminent military operations on a scale the West Bank has not seen in nearly 60 years of occupation.

Within hours, the whole city of 250,000 people had been sealed off and the neighbourhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of Friday’s attack, had been flattened. By Sunday morning, there was nothing left but rubble of an industrial area that had been full of car workshops, a big ceramics plant and other enterprises.

As the bulldozers were at work there, another district a few kilometres away was being systematically emptied. Ein Deir Baha was allegedly home to at least one of the two men involved in the attack (both of whom were killed on the spot), and on Friday its residents paid the price.

The imam from the local mosque, Fahed Ahmaro, was woken at about midnight by the loudspeakers from military vehicles patrolling the street, telling homeowners to vacate their homes immediately for their own safety.

blocks.caption: Fahed Ahmaro, who was forced to flee his home in the Deir Baha area of Hebron by Israeli security forces, looks at his house from a distance.  Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Ahmaro had 30 members of his family living in his house. He rushed his frail mother and some of his grandchildren to his daughter’s house in another part of Hebron, and was on his way back in the hope of picking up some of his possessions when his neighbour phoned him.

“He told me not to come back, and the army had blown up the gates to the house. I don’t know what they have done to it by now. I heard they destroyed the furniture,” Ahmaro said. “You don’t know what you have until you lose it. Now I realise how devastating it is to lose your home.”

blocks.caption: Fahed Ahmaro’s house in Hebron, now a military position, with netting over its upper floors Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: At midday on Sunday, he was in a Hebron market shopping for a change of clothes for his grandchildren, uncertain how long the family’s exile would last.
He had heard that the house was being used as a base by Israeli soldiers and looking up at the house, perched on the side of a steep hill, he could see some lights on but no sign of life.

The Hebron municipality said that 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced by the army sweep through Ein Deir Baha. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said that the displaced population had left voluntarily, that “civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area”.
Ahmaro was outraged at the suggestion that he had any choice about fleeing.
“Never, never, never. Why should I leave my house?” he asked.
Abdul Halim al-Tamimi tried to stay put when the military came at 1.30am. The 77-year-old was told his family had only 10 minutes to vacate their home.

“An intelligence officer told me if we didn’t go, they would displace us the same way they have done it in Gaza,” he said. “We stood there in front of the house, and we refused to leave until we were faced by three military vehicles and they forced us out.”

By the time the Tamimi family left, it was 3am on Saturday morning. On Sunday morning their home was festooned with large Israeli flags and ringed with military vehicles. The army had turned the substantial villa into its headquarters.
In its statement, the Israeli military claimed that 2,000 local people were from the Jaba’a clan, from which the gunmen were allegedly drawn, and which the army claimed was “associated with Hamas”.
The claim drew consternation and derision from people in Ein Deir Baha. They numbered the extent of the Jaba’a clan at 150 at most, with no known reputation for radicalism.

“We are from a completely different family. We are innocent people. We have nothing to do with the whole thing,” Tamimi said. “I don’t know what they are using it for, other than maybe election publicity.”
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no vote in Tuesday’s elections, but their lives could be deeply affected by the outcome.

blocks.caption: Wasam Sadi, a Palestinian driver, has difficulties with his vision after he was attacked in his truck by Israeli settlers near the entrance of Hebron.  Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: By Sunday evening, all roads in and out of the city remained closed to cars, with heavy steel barriers swung across them. The only traffic was on foot, with taxi drivers squabbling for fares. The driver of a delivery truck, Wasam Sadi, pulled in at one checkpoint with the cab windshield smashed and glass fragments in his eyes. He had been attacked by settlers at a nearby junction, he said.

“It’s collective punishment,” said Hebron’s mayor, Yousef al-Jabari. “They have dragged people from their houses, and they have prevented the media from getting into the district in order to cover up what is happening.
“Netanyahu and his gang are using Palestinian land to displace Palestinian people, closing the city, closing the mosque, in order to achieve their political goals.”

articles.title: Man found dead in Queensland floodwaters as state hit by days-long deluge
articles.summary:
Many rivers and roads left flooded after torrential downpours across Queensland

A man’s body has been found in floodwaters following an unusual weather system that delivered multiple storms…

blocks.text: A man’s body has been found in floodwaters following an unusual weather system that delivered multiple storms and a days-long deluge to parts of Australia.
Emergency services were called to a creek at Boompa on Queensland’s Fraser Coast shortly after 11am on Monday after reports a man had been found unresponsive.
The man was declared dead after being found in Smothering Creek on Boompa Road, Queensland Police said.
An investigation into his death has begun, with police to prepare a report for the coroner.
Further south, six campers were rescued after becoming stranded by floodwaters at a public campground in Leyburn in Queensland’s Southern Downs.
Queensland Fire and Rescue Swiftwater crews responded to the call for help at 7.45am on Monday.
They rescued three men aged 71, 47 and 26 and two women aged 68 and 26 without incident around 11.15am.
There were no reports of physical injuries, Queensland Police said in a statement.
Torrential downpours across Queensland between Thursday and Monday left many rivers and roads flooded across the state’s south and east.
There are warnings of more rain and flooding to come.
Flash flooding hit Laidley Creek and Glenore Grove in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane, closing some roads, Queensland police said on Monday.
The highest recorded four-day totals were spread across the state, with Blackdown Tableland, near Rockhampton, recording 439.4mm to early Monday.
Lower Springbrook, near the Gold Coast, recorded 325.2mm, while Nambour, near the Sunshine Coast, copped 314.2mm.
Brooweena, inland of K’gari, received 299.6mm.
Meteorologist Angus Hines said the system behind the downpours was unusual.

“The widespread rain bands with heaps of cloud cover, much cooler temperatures, and then the storms in that situation are really driven by what’s going on in the higher parts of the atmosphere,” he said.
On Sunday evening, thunderstorms were briefly connected from southern Queensland to Bass Strait, as a swift-moving system passed towards Australia’s east coast.
The storm band raced over most states, propelled by strong winds in the upper atmosphere.
“But that steering wind sort of just tapered off through the night last night over [Queensland’s] Darling Downs,” Hines said.
Flood warnings are current for Warrill Creek and the Bremer River in the Lockyer Valley, the Macintyre and Moonie rivers in the south, and the Mary River near the Sunshine Coast.
Western Queensland also remains on alert, with warnings current for the Warrego River at Charleville, the Bulloo River in Quilpie, and the Barcoo River at Blackall.
The Bureau of Meteorology said Queensland’s weather was set to return to more typical spring conditions as the week continued.
Hot and humid days are expected to give way to more subdued afternoon showers and storms.

articles.title: Brazil keeps left: what Lula’s victory means for his country and beyond
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: As Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured victory in the presidential race, we look the implications for democracy, the environment and international relations

Good…

blocks.text: Good morning. Chances are you woke this morning to news of two momentous election results. In Serbia, a student-led movement has ousted the country’s long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić (which you can read more about here). And just hours ago, Brazil’s president staged a sensational turnaround against his far-right opponent after a nail-biting vote.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, won a forth nonconsecutive term as president, seeing off far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who spearheaded the radical populist movement built by his father and former president, Jair. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election.

After Bolsonaro’s surprise first-round victory earlier this month, the Workers’ party incumbent Lula pulled off a historic fightback – a consolidation of the democratic resurgence the country has enjoyed since he took office – and an early birthday present for the veteran leftist, who turns 81 on Tuesday.

But with Bolsonaro refusing to accept the result, the victory is a tense one. I spoke to the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips, who was in São Paulo at the Workers’ party vote count, to find out what the result means and what may lie ahead.
Weekend roundup

items: UK news | Two people have been killed and more than 160,000 properties have been left without power as Storm Boelo continues to batter the UK.
Crime | British police are recording a growing number of crimes linked to cocaine, including assaults, domestic abuse and dangerous driving, as figures show consumption has surged across England.

France | Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.

UK politics | Prime minister Andy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers including Angela Rayner but risks causing concern among fellow red wall MPs.
Aviation | Three in four European airline pilots have taken microsleeps in the cockpit, while almost a quarter routinely fly despite being too fatigued to work, according to a report.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘This is the crescendo of Lula’s incredible, if sometimes controversial, 50-year political career’

blocks.caption: This morning’s results were an unprecedented turnaround, according to election analysts. Photograph: Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

blocks.text: When the results were declared just after midnight UK time, the choice of Brazil’s 159 million voters was narrow, but clear. The 80-year-old leftist received 51.79% of the vote to his rival’s 48.21% – about 4.3m votes – in what Lula called “a defeat for denialism”.
A visibly angry Bolsonaro has already refused to concede, citing a decision to extend voting for an extra two hours – although both sides had called for it, for different reasons.
The outcome was an unprecedented turnaround after a populist surge in first-round voting at the beginning of the month left Brazil’s progressives reeling.

In those early October elections, Flávio Bolsonaro received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – putting the 45-year-old scion of the authoritarian clan in pole position: not once, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
In the intervening weeks, the polls tightened dramatically, putting Bolsonaro ahead by only fractions of a percentage point.

“This is the crescendo of an incredible, if sometimes controversial, 50-year political career,” Tom says. I can hear crowds of Lula supporters cheering in the background as we speak, and fireworks exploding. “It saw Lula go from rural poverty to union leader to the first elected working-class leader of Brazil, who has helped millions of people escape poverty and rode a commodities boom in his first two terms”.

For Brazil, a Lula win represents stability and the assurance that the country’s democratic future is secure, at least in the short term. “Over the past four years, Lula has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by more than 70%. He’s come to the help of the Indigenous people who live there. He’s cracked down on illegal mining,” Tom tells me. “It’s very positive news is that all this will continue.”
How did Lula turn things around?

“Bolsonarismo is a far-right movement … that has put down deep roots in Brazilian society,” Bernardo Mello Franco, a political columnist for the Rio broadsheet O Globo, told Tom earlier this month, pointing to a series of societal shifts have contributed to this.
Evangelical Christianity has expanded across Brazil in recent decades, with church leaders throwing their support behind the socially conservative policies favoured by Bolsanaro Sr and Jr.

Pro-gun Flavio Bolsonaro harnessed voter frustration at chronic levels of urban crime and violence. Despite being embedded in Brazilian politics for decades, he successfully portrayed himself as an anti-establishment outsider, using social media far more effectively than his rival.

And others believe he had significant help: a dozen watchdogs and research groups have published reports alleging that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign. The controversy grew after Brazils’ electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”, while the company called the allegations “false and unfounded”.

Progressives were galvanised after the first-round results revealed a record abstention rate of 21%, more common among Lula-supporting groups such as lower-income voters, and their focus sharpened on mobilisation. Millions joined a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s army”, which sent out daily instructions on how to make supportive content go viral. The 80-year-old incumbent, who only took ownership of his first smartphone in recent days, started posting to Instagram and TikTok. For the first time, the president’s digital reach overtook that of Bolsonaro.

Meanwhile, the Bolsonaro campaign was hit by a succession of scandals. In a revelation that made the UK’s partygate seem tame by comparison, last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of the 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party along with sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to cut deals with his father’s government.

Amid speculation that a comeback might be possible, at a million-strong rally on Copacabana beach in Rio on Saturday, activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “We are going to turn this around!”
And so he did.
What role did Trump play in the election?

The US president has boasted about “lots of people that I got elected” in Latin America, styling himself as a kingmaker after a succession of right-wing candidates aligned with Washington have won power.

Although Donald Trump did not openly endorse Flávio Bolsonaro, his influence loomed large. Last year, he denounced the supreme court trial of his ally Jair Bolsonaro as a “witch-hunt”, imposing extraordinary 50% tariffs on Brazilian imports as retribution for what he claimed was political persecution.

Lula has styled himself as the country’s defender against Trump’s “colonial” designs. His victory consolidates a multilateral foreign policy and pragmatic approach to relations with the US, China and Russia. He has rejected invitations to join the controversial coalition of Latin American countries conducting military operations against drug cartels alongside the Pentagon, which would have resulted in much greater US involvement on Brazilian soil.

Furthermore, a win for pro-democracy campaigners in one country may serve to bolster international counterparts. As our senior international correspondent Julian Borger sets out in this compelling piece, along with the Brazil vote, a series of high-stakes elections in Serbia yesterday, Israel on Tuesday and the US next week are closely interlinked, and Lula’s win may have global ramifications, as leaders across Latin America and the world congratulate him this morning.
What does the result mean for the environment, in Brazil and beyond?

Last week, Tom travelled to Roraima, the northern state where Bolsonaro registered his best result nationwide. On his trip, he heard first-hand from Indigenous leaders and conservationists on why the populist’s success was causing panic.

His father’s environmentally devastating administration facilitated an illegal gold rush – turbo-charged by record global gold prices – that ravaged the Yanomami Indigenous reserve on the northern reaches of the Amazon.

When Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, the left-winger launched an environmentalist mission to expel the illegal miners, taking on the multibillion dollar extraction industry. Alongside wider green policies, he reduced deforestation in the Amazon to record lows.
“Tragically,” says Tom, “the environment only came up in the final presidential debate of this campaign.”

“Given that the Amazon makes up such a large portion of Brazil, and how important that region is to the global climate crisis, it’s amazing that it’s not been debated more. But people were voting more on economy, public security and culture war issues.”
In that final debate last Friday, Tom says that Lula “tried to show off the excellent, if incomplete, work that his government’s done in protecting the environment”.
Many will be relieved at Bolsonaro’s loss, as his vision for the Amazon was almost identical to his father’s.

While a Lula victory brings hope that these policies will continue, he will be working with a newly elected congress that features a record number of rightwing politicians hostile to Indigenous rights and environmental issues.
How will Bolsonaro respond?
after newsletter promotion
The immediate aftermath of the election results is likely to be fraught, warns Tom, with Flávio Bolsonaro saying it was “impossible to concede the election result”.

“The Bolsonaro response is exactly as I feared but I don’t think it will mean very much,” Tom says. “All these world leaders are now recognising Lula’s win and I don’t think Bolsonaro has a hope of overturning this result”.

Tom suspects that in the coming days Bolsonaro will head to the States, to avoid ongoing criminal investigations. “That’s not to say there might not be violence from his supporters, but his political career is done. The fact they’ve lost is a sign that the name ‘Bolsonaro’ is toxic for a slight majority of Brazilian people.”
The week to come

items: Tuesday | Israel goes to the polls on Tuesday, amid orders from prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu for a full lockdown of the occupied West Bank after recent checkpoint attacks. His government will be fighting for its survival.

Wednesday | On Wednesday Chancellor John Healey will deliver his first budget statement in the House of Commons, which is expected to give local authorities more spending powers, as a means to promote growth

Thursday and Friday | European and Canadian leaders will meet in Montreal for the 21st EU-Canada summit, to discuss security and strategic cooperation. It will be the first opportunity for leaders to iron out details over a proposed invitation for Canada to become the EU’s first ever “associate member”

The front pages

Today in Focus

blocks.caption: Who ultimately has benefited from the UAE’s investment in Manchester?  Illustration: Anaïs Mims/Getty

blocks.text: How Abu Dhabi bought Andy Burnham’s Manchester
Today in Focus presenter and city resident Helen Pidd walks through modern Manchester – where Burnham was mayor for nearly a decade – and charts its transformation wrought by Emirati money.

Helen talks to North of England editor Josh Halliday too about how Abu Dhabi came to Manchester, alleged “sweetheart deals” it struck to own so much land, and a lack of transparency about it all even now.
Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld

blocks.caption: Illustration: Tom Gauld/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Cory’s shearwater fledglings on Corvo Island in the Azores.  Photograph: Andrea Zanenga

blocks.text: Every autumn, Corvo Island in the Azores turns off its public lighting for a few key days to help fledgling seabirds fly to the ocean guided by the stars.

Since 2019, the 450 or so inhabitants of the smallest and most northerly island of Portugal’s Azores archipelago have switched off the lights for five nights to tackle the disastrous effects of artificial light on Cory’s shearwaters. The campaign started after the community noticed huge numbers of deaths among young shearwaters, who spend three months in their nests before attempting their first flight to the ocean. Many are fatally confused by the artificial glow of streetlights, and end up crashing on the streets of the island’s only village, Vila do Corvo. By going dark, the stars can be seen clearly, allowing the juvenile birds safe passage to the ocean.

articles.title: Who should win the men's Ballon d'Or? BBC Sport pundits have their say
articles.summary: The Ballon d'Or winner will be announced in London on Monday - but who is going to claim the showpiece award?

blocks.text: European football expert Julien Laurens: I think he was the best player in Europe last season, especially in the Champions League where he was outstanding. He helped lead the team to another title, a back-to-back one.

He got the penalty in the final, scored in both semi-finals, in the quarter-final, and in the last 16. He was amazing in those huge, huge games where you want your best players to step up. He deserves to win the Ballon d'Or for being the best player in the world all the way up to the World Cup.

He won't win it, unfortunately, because Lamine Yamal, for the player he is and how entertaining and spectacular he is, didn't really shine at the World Cup, even if Spain won it. He didn't really do that well in the Champions League for Barcelona, getting knocked out early. However, his style of football means he'll probably win it - but it should be Kvaratskhelia.

Ex-Liverpool and Blackburn full-back Stephen Warnock: I think it will be Lamine Yamal for helping Spain to win the World Cup. If you were asking who else is in the hunt, I would say Michael Olise, but my pick personally would be Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, he is unbelievable. I love watching him play. He had such an impact for Paris St-Germain and last season he was incredible. I just don't think he will get the votes with Georgia not being in the World Cup.

BBC Radio 5 Live Euro Leagues guest and Athletic reporter Rory Smith: It will probably go to Lamine Yamal because it generally goes to someone who has won the biggest trophy, and this is the World Cup. It shouldn't be him because he wasn't necessarily Spain's most important player but his fame and talent means it will be him.

Personally I would give it to Kvaratskhelia. He has been the most exciting player in European club football for a while now, a valuable part of the PSG team who retained the Champions League, and crucially I think you shouldn't suffer because you come from a country who isn't in the running to win the World Cup.

articles.title: Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies aged 46
articles.summary: Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme.

blocks.text: Eric Bauza, the voice artist behind Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died aged 46.
A statement from the Emmy award-winning star's family posted on Instagram, external said he had died "suddenly".
Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme, and appeared in the recent release Forgotten Island.
Variety reports that the cause of death was hypertensive cardiovascular disease and that Bauza died at home on Sunday.
In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza, who was born in Ontario and was of Filipino descent, said he grew up a huge fan of the Looney Tunes characters and used to copy the voices as a child.
"Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures," he said, external. "It doesn't matter what part of the planet you're from. You get the comedy."
He voiced Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd and Foghorn Leghorn in 2021's Space Jam: A New Legacy before reprising those roles and that of Road Runner in Coyote vs. Acme.
He also played the part of Toad General in 2023's The Super Mario Bros. Movie and its sequel The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, the fifth highest-grossing film internationally this year.
Between 2022 and 2025, he won three Emmy awards for outstanding voice performance in a number of TV series.

In a statement reported by the Hollywood Reporter, external, Channing Dungey, the chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks, said: "Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world.
"He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life."

articles.title: Labour urged to plug predicted £400m shortfall in overseas aid funding in 2027
articles.summary:
Official forecast indicates shortfall below 0.3% of national income in promised official development assistance

The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on…

blocks.text: The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.
Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.
The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.

However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.
Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.

Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.

The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget.
The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.
The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.
Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.
She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.
“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.
“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”
after newsletter promotion
Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.

The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.
The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.

The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.

The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.

An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.
“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

articles.title: Australian murderer loses bid to eat Vegemite in prison
articles.summary: Andre McKechnie, who murdered a property developer, argued it was his right to enjoy Australian culture.

blocks.text: A convicted murderer serving a life sentence in Australia has lost his bid to overturn a ban on prisoners consuming Vegemite - the salty yeast-based spread that has become a national symbol.
Andre McKechnie argued that the ban, in place since 2006, denied him the right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian".
Authorities in the state of Victoria say inmates may use the strong-smelling paste to disguise contraband substances or to brew alcohol behind bars.
And on Monday, a Supreme Court judge rejected McKechnie's appeal, saying the prisoner's "cultural rights are limited primarily by the fact he has been sentenced to a term of imprisonment".

In his lawsuit against Victoria's Department of Justice and Corrections, the agency which manages the state's prisons, McKechnie, 54, said the ban on the spread breached law requiring prisons to provide food that allowed inmates to maintain their health and well-being but the judge said that had not been proven.
McKechnie was handed a life sentence for stabbing a property developer to death in Queensland in the 1990s. He served part of his sentence in Queensland before being transferred to Victoria.
During the hearing, the court heard evidence from Corrections Victoria that the smell of vegemite can distract sniffer dogs trying to detect drugs being brought into prison.
The product is also banned in jails in Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania.
A much-loved breakfast spread for some, Vegemite has acquired controversial accolades since it first hit shop shelves in Australia in 1923.
The thick, brown spread was invented in the Victorian capital of Melbourne more than a century ago as an alternative to the British spread Marmite.

It sparked an international dispute in April last year when an Australian cafe owner in Canada was told to remove jars of the condiment from his shelves as it did not comply with local health regulations.

Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese intervened in the row, saying it was "rather odd" that Canada allowed the sale of Vegemite's "rubbish" rival product Marmite. The cafe owner was later allowed to continue selling the spread.

Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election

blocks.caption: Lula has won a fourth presidential term after a historic upset Image: Brian Snyder/REUTERS

blocks.text: Brazilian leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, electoral authorities said.

Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

The campaign was marred by scandals and mudslinging. Sunday’s vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula’s claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.

Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.

In regards to foreign policy in his next term, Lula will have to manage relations with Washington while maintaining his anti-imperialist stance, as the Trump administration increasingly asserts its influence across the region. Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.

articles.title: India's cartoonists built an audience online - now their posts are being restricted
articles.summary: Indian cartoonists say online restrictions are making satire harder, but they aren't giving up.

blocks.text: Image source, Satish Acharya
Satish Acharya is among Indian cartoonists whose work has been restricted by Meta recently
ByNikita Yadav
BBC News, Delhi
For the second time in three weeks, Indian cartoonist Satish Acharya found himself effectively invisible on Instagram in his own country.
The 55-year-old discovered on Tuesday that his account had once again been briefly blocked in India, allegedly with no explanation from the platform.

Just a few weeks ago, another cartoonist, Manjul, had found that Instagram had restricted a post criticising India's election commission over its controversial revision of voter rolls. His profile remained accessible.

The cases have raised concerns about the use of legal orders to restrict political satire in India, with cartoonists saying they are often given little explanation for why their work has been blocked.
Acharaya's account was first restricted from 28 September to 6 October, when users in India could neither find his profile through search nor access it through a web link.
Anyone trying to access his profile saw a message saying it was unavailable under India's Information Technology Rules.
The rules allow authorities and courts to order social media platforms to remove or restrict content.
The government says they help tackle unlawful material, but artists and free-speech advocates warn they can stifle India's rich tradition of political satire.
"Meta platforms have been restricting the reach of my cartoons for some years," Acharya told the BBC. "But when my entire profile was restricted in India, I was a little sad."

He wrote to Meta, Instagram's parent company, but received no reply. He says he was preparing to go to court when his account became accessible again in early October, only to be blocked again earlier this week for three days.
In a statement, Meta told the BBC that may temporarily restrict accounts to comply with India's IT Rules but did not explain the specific reasons for restricting Acharya's account or Manjul's post.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The message on Satish Acharya's profile when it was last blocked between 20-22 October

blocks.text: The message on Satish Acharya's profile when it was last blocked between 20-22 October
Critics say the restrictions come as humour and satire play an increasingly visible role in political dissent in India, particularly among younger people.

Memes and Gen-Z humour helped fuel protests over education and jobs in July, which led to the resignation of India's education minister. Online debate has also intensified over a controversial revision of voter rolls that removed 130 million names.

The political significance of social media has not been lost on the government. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has urged ministers to strengthen their online presence and connect with younger audiences.
At the same time, technology policy expert Prateek Waghre says the government is increasingly using legal orders to regulate online content.

The Indian Express reported, external that government agencies sent nearly 195,000 blocking and content-restriction orders to platforms including Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July through the federal government's Sahyog portal.
The figures, obtained through a right-to-information request, do not show how many posts were ultimately restricted or removed. The BBC has not seen the original response.

Waghre says that some platforms, particularly Meta, "seem more willing to comply", he says, while X appears more willing to push back. But limited public data makes comparisons difficult. Meta declined to comment on his assessment.
The government has also reportedly sought greater scrutiny of how social media platforms recommend content.

Earlier this week, several media outlets reported, external that authorities had asked Meta to ensure its systems did not steer users towards "a single or limited set of narratives" and strengthen checks on content that could "cause public disorder or incite violence".
The BBC has sought comment from India's IT ministry on the restrictions and reported instructions to Meta but has not received a response.

blocks.caption: Image caption, RK Laxman is among the most recognisable political cartoonists in India

blocks.text: Image source, India Today Group via Getty Images
RK Laxman is among the most recognisable political cartoonists in India
Of course, political satire has a long history in India - as do attempts to curb it.
Cartoons have been a fixture of Indian journalism since independence, with RK Laxman's Common Man becoming one of its most recognisable characters.

But cartoonists have also faced censorship. During the Emergency in the 1970s, when civil liberties were suspended and the press was tightly controlled, Abu Abraham continued drawing, even as dozens of his cartoons were stamped "not passed by censors".
In 2012, cartoonist Aseem Trivedi was arrested on sedition charges over cartoons allegedly mocking the Indian constitution. The charges were later dropped.

Today, concerns about restrictions on political expression extend beyond cartoonists. India ranks 157th in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, while critics accuse the government of putting growing pressure on independent media. The government rejects the criticism, saying India's media remains free and vibrant.
Comedians have also faced controversy over political satire. Kunal Kamra, known for his jokes about Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his party, has faced threats, cancelled shows and legal action.
For cartoonists, however, challenging those in power is central to their work.
"We are among the default opposition," says Sandeep Adhwaryu, a cartoonist at a leading Indian newspaper.
"The nature of the craft is to oppose," he says, adding that cartoonists, like journalists, must question whoever holds power.
Acharya says he has followed that principle throughout his career. Before 2014, many of his cartoons targeted the Congress-led government and were shared by BJP leaders.
"I never faced official restrictions on my cartoons during the previous governments, though there would be some trolling occasionally," he says.
Now, with the BJP in power, much of his satire is directed at Modi's government.

blocks.caption: Image caption, One of Manjul's cartoons which criticised the controversial voter roll revision that has resulted in the removal of 130 million names from the electoral rolls

blocks.text: Image source, Manjul
One of Manjul's cartoons which criticised the controversial voter roll revision that has resulted in the removal of 130 million names from the electoral rolls
Social media has allowed independent cartoonists like Acharya to reach audiences without relying on newspapers or other traditional outlets.
"We are not associated with newspapers or any mainstream media. That's why we can draw," says Manjul.
But that freedom comes with a new vulnerability - dependence on platforms that can restrict their work or cut off access to their audiences.
No one knows this better than Rachita Taneja, the creator of the hugely popular Instagram comic Sanitary Panels.
"My career would not have existed without the internet," she told the BBC. Yet she describes social media as a double-edged sword.
"At the end of the day it's a for-profit endeavour that answers to advertisers," she says.
Taneja says that Meta's compliance with Indian government requests reflects the company's commercial priorities rather than concern for users' rights. Meta declined to comment.

Even cartoonists working in traditional newsrooms face pressure. Adhwaryu says artists may soften captions, avoid certain subjects or think twice before submitting a cartoon. Over time, he says, such self-censorship can become normalised, even without explicit instructions.
Still, cartoonists have found ways to support one another.

When Acharya's Instagram account was first restricted, Taneja drew a stick-figure cartoon in solidarity. "Seeing people on the front lines creating communities, protesting, running campaigns, tirelessly fighting for their own rights and the rights of others is what keeps me going," she says.
Adhwaryu believes satire will continue to adapt. He compares cartoons and humour to a "shape-shifting virus".
"It keeps mutating in response to its environment," he says. "It will find its way."

articles.title: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders
articles.summary:
The fifth plenum comes against a backdrop of years of purges that have had some analysts wondering if the issue is corruption or a lack of loyalty

When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he…

blocks.text: When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.

As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials prepare for an important meeting this week discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.

The “fifth plenum” starts on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption.

As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.

Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.
He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.

Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.

Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.

blocks.caption: Xi Jinping at a gathering at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing last week.  Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.

The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.

The upcoming meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.

Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.

In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.
The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.

In January, Zhang Youxia, China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)
A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.
Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.

Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.

Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.
